item.title: Proximal Difference-in-Differences for Causal Learning under Confounding and Outcome Drift
item.description: arXiv:2611.10310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating long-term treatment effects is essential in regulatory and healthcare decision-making, yet the limited follow-up duration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) poses a significant challenge. Open-label extension studies attempt to capture additional information for treated subjects, but there is often significant systematic censoring and selection bias due to placebo crossover. While supplementing RCTs with real-world evidence is a common strategy, existing methods often rely on restrictive exchangeability assumptions that fail under latent confounding. We propose a novel proximal framework to integrate real-world evidence into an RCT with an open-label extension to estimate the long-term continued-control trajectory. Our approach successfully identifies long-term effects even in the presence of time-varying latent confounding effects and inter-study outcome drift. We provide a doubly robust locally efficient estimator that provides further resilience to model misspecification. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework maintains validity in complex data-generating processes where standard approaches may be biased.
item.dc:creator: Sihyung Park, Shu Yang, Ilya Lipkovich, Wenyu Ye, Mingyang Shan

item.title: SAMBoost: Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting
item.description: arXiv:2611.10373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose SAMBoost (Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting), a gradient boosting method that combines tree-based covariate modelling with a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) latent spatial field through a single penalised objective. At each boosting iteration, the predictor is decomposed into separate covariate and spatial components. The method is motivated by applications in which the spatial effect is not a nuisance to be removed but a quantity of interest that must be recovered alongside the covariates. In insurance, for example, practitioners need both flexible nonlinear covariate effects and an interpretable geographic risk surface that can be reported on its own. Existing approaches often involve trade-offs, offering flexible covariate modelling but no explicit spatial field, rigorous spatial inference with a fixed additive covariate structure, or a combination of both at computational costs that limit practicality for large datasets. SAMBoost addresses these goals within the boosting loop, and the underlying mesh produces a sparse precision structure whose cost is largely independent of sample size. On simulations and on an open benchmark, SAMBoost matches or improves on the predictive accuracy of joint Gaussian process and tree boosting approaches. It is also faster and recovers the spatial field and covariate effects more accurately. When covariate effects include interactions, it outperforms additive Bayesian spatial models. Applied to a flood insurance portfolio with 4.9 million records, SAMBoost trains on the full training set without subsampling and runs about sixteen times faster than a Bayesian reference, with a consistent spatial risk surface. A public Python implementation is available.
item.dc:creator: Mulah Moriah, Franck Vermet, Pierre Ailliot, Juliette Legrand

item.title: Causal Discovery Grounding and the Naturalness Assumption
item.description: arXiv:2611.10388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard causal discovery postulates that structure can be described by a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which can be partially reconstructed by using the faithfulness principle. According to this principle, conditional independencies in the observational distribution correspond exactly to those encoded in the unknown DAG. However, such algorithms are challenged by the fact that, without even stronger assumptions, approximate failures of faithfulness are empirically undistinguishable from exact ones. This leaves an inferential gap which can lead to major implications to causal effect identification. We introduce a different perspective, not reliant on exact independencies. By considering the specialized problem of discovering whether unmeasured confounding can be ruled out for a particular cause-effect pair, we introduce a principle we call naturalness, in which the strength of observational associations bounds the strength of causal dependencies. The bounding function is unknown, with degrees of freedom not present in faithfulness. We model uncertainty about this function using a Bayesian framing which allows for the use of experiments from separate studies, grounding an adaptive causal discovery principle on historical experimental data. We demonstrate its usefulness in partial identification of causal effects, and discuss how the promising results can motivate new principles for general causal discovery.
item.dc:creator: Guilherme P. Soares, Andreas Koukorinis, Sander Beckers, Jake Fawkes, David S. Watson, Ricardo Silva

item.title: Efficient Estimation and Consistent Class Number Selection for Semiparametric Class-Specific Index Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.10401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The study introduces a parsimonious semiparametric class-specific index regression that captures heterogeneous covariate--response relationships across latent subpopulations. In such a latent class model formulation, subject-specific indices are used as a complete-data representation of the realized latent labels. We propose a unified framework for estimating model parameters and recovering latent class memberships. For the class-specific index mean model, estimation and latent class recovery are conducted via a pseudo-least-squares criterion with a separation penalty, and a semiparametric information criterion is proposed for consistently estimating the number of classes. Exploiting the response distribution, we develop a Bayes classification rule that maximizes the asymptotic probability of correct assignment and a pseudo-maximum likelihood criterion that yields class index coefficient estimators with asymptotic semiparametric efficiency. This refinement step characterizes latent class membership probabilities via sufficient dimension reduction of the covariate space. Simulations and applications to marketing and biomedical datasets demonstrate superior finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology in parameter estimation, latent class recovery, and class number selection.
item.dc:creator: Jen-Chieh Teng, Sheng-Hsin Fan, Chin-Tsang Chiang, Alvin Lim

item.title: Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares
item.description: arXiv:2611.10459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many scientific responses take values in Riemannian manifolds, with predictors that are scalar- and/or manifold-valued. A regression analysis in such settings must provide accurate prediction with hypothesis testing for individual coefficients. Yet no current manifold-regression framework accommodates both predictor types and enables per-coefficient hypothesis tests. We propose Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares (ROLS) as a tangent space conditional-mean model, which is the ordinary least squares (OLS) analogue for Riemannian manifolds. ROLS is well-defined under an explicit injectivity condition that keeps the logarithm maps single-valued, with cut-locus conditions for branch-sensitive cases outside it. Within the local geometric setting it admits a closed-form estimator, an $O(n^{-1})$ excess prediction-error bound with explicit curvature bias, and asymptotic $t$- and Wald tests for individual coefficients. With synthetic simulations and three real-data case studies, ROLS is shown to be competitive with the state-of-the-art baselines. In addition, the per-coefficient tests agree with effects reported in literature. We envision ROLS to be a standard tool for manifold-valued regression with coefficient-level inference to support scientific discovery, which can be interpreted in the same way as Euclidean OLS. The source code is available at https://github.com/XiaoyuChenPub/ROLS.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Xiaoyu Chen, Yujing (Zipan) Huang, Yingyan Zeng. Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2026
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Chen, Yujing Huang, Yingyan Zeng

item.title: Generalized Laplacian in Spectral Seriation on Manifold Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.10494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Noisy high-dimensional observations may have conditional means lying on a smooth closed curve, indexed by temporal labels or phases. We want to recover the latent phases for each observation and thus retrieve a circular ordering. Spectral seriation uses the graph Laplacian's spectral embedding to recover the phases and ordering. We consider generalized graph Laplacians in spectral seriation, where a parameter $\alpha$ controls the degree normalization and affects the accuracy and stability of both tasks. We develop and compare three generalized Laplacian constructions: a shifted generalized Laplacian, a graph-difference Laplacian, and an extra-normalized generalized Laplacian. Among these, the extra-normalized variant is less sensitive to the choice of $\alpha$ and achieves the strongest overall recovery performance. For this variant, we establish a theoretical error bound relating phase estimation accuracy to eigenspace perturbation, accounting for the inherent rotation and reflection ambiguity. In synthetic experiments across various scenarios, our new graph Laplacian outperforms the classic spectral seriation method and other seriation methods. On the Pink Angel data, which records photos from different viewpoints, our method achieves zero ordering error and the lowest phase recovery error. On FUCCI cell-cycle data, our method performs the best when all 6 cells are mixed, demonstrating the robustness to heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Ruizi Wu, Wanjie Wang, Jinchi Lv

item.title: A General Statistical Framework for Attention and Manipulation Checks
item.description: arXiv:2611.10515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attention and manipulation checks are widely used in survey experiments to assess respondents' attentiveness and engagement with treatment, respectively. Yet these checks are subject to measurement error, which may itself depend on treatment when checks are administered after treatment exposure. Restricting analyses to respondents who pass these checks can therefore introduce substantial bias. We propose a general statistical framework for analyzing survey experiments with pre- or post-treatment attention and manipulation checks while accounting for measurement error. We show that three separate checks suffice to identify the proportion of respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment, provided that the checks are conditionally independent among treated respondents given their true, unobserved attentiveness or manipulation status and pre-treatment covariates. Under additional mild assumptions, this result also identifies the average treatment effect among respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment. Building on these identification results, we propose an estimator that allows flexible covariate modeling and establish its asymptotic normality. Applications to framing and digital media literacy experiments demonstrate how accounting for measurement error yields treatment effect estimates that are substantively different from those obtained using conventional approaches.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Nakamura, Kosuke Imai

item.title: Weak-Instrument Inference and Model Diagnostics in Double Machine Learning for Linear Instrumental Variable Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.10863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study weak-instrument-robust inference in partially linear instrumental-variables models with learned nuisances. Building on an i.i.d. uniform-size baseline, we establish uniform asymptotic validity of clustered cross-fitted Anderson-Rubin inference and cross-fitted score inference under the stated sampling and nuisance-rate conditions. Extensions establish Anderson-Rubin validity for survey-weighted target laws and fold-nested generated instruments. A supporting population benchmark shows that prediction-optimal instrument residualization maximizes concentration when the treatment nuisance is correctly specified. A five-design diagnostic portfolio, a known-truth Monte Carlo, and an exploratory selector examine how nuisance specification and estimation affect realized strength and inference.
item.dc:creator: Airui Meng

item.title: Forecasting Replication Study Results from Meta-Analyses
item.description: arXiv:2611.10943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multisite replication projects often rely on published meta-analyses to plan their sample sizes, but meta-analyses tend to overestimate population effects because of publication bias and differences in study characteristics. We developed methods to forecast site-level estimates of a not-yet-conducted replication from a meta-analysis. Extending calibrated estimates from meta-regression, we constructed nonparametric prediction intervals that condition on each site's moderator levels and correct for publication bias through inverse-probability-of-publication weighting under an assumed severity. These intervals achieve nominal coverage asymptotically when population effects are normally distributed, with a bounded coverage error otherwise. We compared four forecasting models (intercept-only meta-analysis or meta-regression, each with and without publication bias correction) in simulation study (81 scenarios and blinded retrospective forecasts of two multisite replications in infant cognition: ManyBabies 1 (104 sites) and ManyBabies 4 (33 sites). Correcting for publication bias improved interval calibration, with gains that increased with bias severity. Meta-regression improved forecasts only when measured moderators explained effect variation and replication sites differed meaningfully on them. In practice, publication bias correction should be the default when forecasting replications from meta-analyses, and replication projects that deliberately vary measured moderators across sites would enable more informative forecasts.
item.dc:creator: Yi Li, Alvin Wei Ming Tan, Francesco Margoni, Michael C. Frank, Maya B. Mathur

item.title: Causal Outcome Learning with Noisy Proxies
item.description: arXiv:2611.10955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern observational biomedical datasets contain increasingly extensive baseline and outcome measurements, yet detecting a clinically meaningful treatment effect remains difficult because investigators must identify an outcome that captures treatment response while adjusting for confounding distributed across numerous noisy baseline variables. We introduce SCOUT (Score-based Causal Outcome Learning Using Treatment signals), a framework that learns a clinically interpretable, treatment-responsive outcome while adjusting for confounding throughout the learning process. SCOUT constructs low-dimensional adjustment representations of high-dimensional baseline measurements to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) and conditional average treatment effect (CATE) for the learned outcome. Importantly, the final adjustment space is at most two-dimensional, allowing treatment-effect heterogeneity to be estimated in this space rather than in the full high-dimensional covariate space. SCOUT also introduces a fourth-order statistic for testing treatment-effect heterogeneity that emphasizes unusually large deviations from the ATE. In synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments, the algorithm achieved competitive ATE estimation accuracy and substantially lower CATE estimation error. In an observational study of patients with bipolar disorder, SCOUT identified a clinically recognizable lithium-associated adverse-effect profile, detecting both a significant ATE (Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.0026) and significant treatment-effect heterogeneity (Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.033).These results demonstrate how jointly learning outcomes and controlling for confounding can facilitate the discovery of treatment effects in high-dimensional observational data.
item.dc:creator: Eric V. Strobl

item.title: A Unified Framework for Robust Blinded Sample Size Re-estimation Based on Nuisance Parameters
item.description: arXiv:2611.10957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blinded sample size re-estimation aims to mitigate uncertainty in nuisance parameters at the design stage while preserving the integrity of the trial. It allows the required sample size to be updated without revealing treatment assignments and thereby reduces the risk of an inappropriate sample size. Although numerous procedures have been proposed for different outcome types, a unified framework is still lacking. We therefore develop a general framework for blinded sample size re-estimation based on nuisance parameters. Within this general framework, we develop robust methods to reduce the influence of extreme observations. The proposed framework combines asymptotically linear estimators for the parameter of interest with robust Z-estimators for nuisance parameters, thereby unifying a broad class of existing procedures through different choices of estimating functions. We also propose a general principle for constructing nuisance parameters that can be estimated from blinded data. The proposed framework is supported by asymptotic theory showing that the type I error rate converges to the nominal level under regularity conditions. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method maintains reliable type I error control across a range of settings, including contaminated data and small pilot sample sizes. Compared with existing blinded and unblinded methods, the proposed framework is more flexible and less sensitive to outliers. A clinical trial application illustrates its practical utility.
item.dc:creator: Long-Hao Xu, Lei Li, Tim Friede

item.title: Overlap-Excluded Estimation of Participation Probabilities for Non-Probability Samples
item.description: arXiv:2611.10962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Correction of selection bias is crucial for making valid statistical inferences about a finite population using non-probability datasets. Various approaches have been proposed to correct this bias and obtain estimates of finite population quantities such as means and totals. The quasi-randomisation approaches, in particular, aim to estimate a `participation probability' for units in the non-probability dataset. These probabilities are then applied in an inverse probability weighting scheme to produce population estimates. In this paper, we propose to estimate the participation probabilities for the non-probability sample by combining the non-probability sample with an available probability sample, while excluding the overlapping units in the probability sample. When the true overlap cannot be determined, we show how the Expectation-Maximization method can be used to simultaneously estimate the overlap and the participation probabilities. We compare the performance of our approach against several alternative methods theoretically and in an empirical context, and demonstrate the efficiency gains that are possible when the overlapping probability sample is excluded.
item.dc:creator: Lyndon Ang, Robert Clark, Bronwyn Loong, Anders Holmberg

item.title: Inference for Non-Probability Samples Using Error-Prone Auxiliary Information
item.description: arXiv:2611.10975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-probability samples are a potential source of rich information for making statistical inferences. However, these datasets often suffer from quality issues, in particular selection bias. The data from a non-probability sample may be combined with auxiliary information from the population or from a reference probability sample to address this bias. The auxiliary information present on these other sources is generally considered to be error-free, however this is not always the case. In this paper, we present a novel semiparametric approach to estimate the participation probabilities of units on a non-probability sample while accounting for error-prone auxiliary information in the reference data source. The approach combines a logistic regression model for the participation probabilities with a nonparametric kernel regression model for the error-prone auxiliary variables. Through a simulation study and real-world data analysis we show that our proposed approach effectively mitigates selection bias and accounts for measurement error, while estimates from methods which ignore the measurement error still exhibit some bias. The consistency of the Inverse Probability Weighted estimator produced using the participation probabilities derived from our approach is demonstrated, and a bootstrap variance approach for the estimator is described.
item.dc:creator: Lyndon Ang, Robert Clark, Bronwyn Loong, Anders Holmberg

item.title: Choosing the basis to compare multivariate distributions: bases, copulas and optimal transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.11004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the choice of an orthonormal basis for comparing two probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ through their one-dimensional projections. We show that two distributions have a common copula in a given basis if and only if their optimal transport can be performed componentwise along the directions of that basis. This motivates the notion of componentwise related distributions and leads to a structural analysis of the bases in which such a representation is possible. In particular, we establish an essential uniqueness result for the corresponding orthogonal decomposition and characterize elliptical families through equality in Gelbrich's bound within location-scatter families. For general distributions, we consider the maximum, over all orthonormal bases, of the sum of the squared quadratic Wasserstein distances between the corresponding one-dimensional projections. We prove that the resulting quantity is a metric, induces the same topology as the quadratic Wasserstein distance, and lies between the Gelbrich and Wasserstein distances, with equality in the upper bound precisely for component-wise related distributions. We also derive first-order conditions for an optimal basis and establish stability and almost-sure consistency of empirical optimal bases. Simulations and examples illustrate the computational feasibility and competitive performance of the proposed procedures and suggest new applications of copulas to multivariate distributional comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Eustasio del Barrio, Juan A. Cuesta-Albertos, Carlos Matr\'an, David Rodr\'iguez-V\'itores

item.title: Cause-specific structural nested cumulative survival time models for competing risks, with application to the Antibody Mediated Prevention trials
item.description: arXiv:2611.11008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials randomized participants to VRC01, a broadly neutralizing antibody, or placebo; the primary analysis estimated prevention efficacy against overall HIV-1 acquisition and against acquisition of VRC01-sensitive strains. All participants were offered daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and PrEP uptake in a trial may differ substantially from uptake in other settings. It is therefore of interest to estimate the effect of oral PrEP on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive strains, as well as the counterfactual cumulative incidence of such acquisition under no or limited PrEP uptake. To address these questions, we extend the structural nested cumulative survival time model (SNCSTM), a causal survival model for time-varying treatments, to a cause-specific version. We show that the cause-specific SNCSTM is closely related to the Fine--Gray subdistribution hazard model, and we study identification under two frameworks. The first, based on sequential ignorability, applies when the time-varying treatment is distinct from the randomized assignment, as with oral PrEP use in AMP. The second, based on an instrumental variable, applies when the time-varying treatment represents compliance with the randomized assignment, and it accommodates unmeasured confounding between the time-varying treatment and event time. Under both frameworks, we propose consistent and asymptotically normal estimators of the structural parameters. We apply the methods to HVTN 704/HPTN 085, one of the two AMP trials, to estimate the effects of oral PrEP use and of VRC01 infusions administered every 8 weeks on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive HIV-1 strains. We also estimate the counterfactual strain-specific cumulative incidence curves under no oral PrEP use and under full adherence to the scheduled VRC01 infusions.
item.dc:creator: Yuxiao Li, Yuhao Deng, Bo Zhang

item.title: Heavy tails in Gaussian-process surrogates: process-level profiling degeneracy versus observation-level identifiability
item.description: arXiv:2611.11188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we study heavy-tailed alternatives to Gaussian-process surrogates, namely Student-$t$ processes, $\alpha$-stable processes and Gaussian processes with heavy-tailed noise. These are Gaussian scale mixtures, and the position of the mixing variable decides whether the tails can be learned from a single realization. For process-level mixtures with a free amplitude, the profile likelihood of the mixing law is data-free and is maximized by the Gaussian law, the plug-in predictive is a data-free transformation of the Gaussian-process predictive, and no estimator can be consistent for the mixing law over the model along one path. For observation-level mixtures with symmetric $\alpha$-stable noise, the tail index is identifiable. Further, for one-dimensional inputs under fixed-domain asymptotics with $\alpha_0<2$ and compact hyperparameter sets, a cross-fitted plug-in estimator and the Laplace marginal-likelihood estimate computed at the global posterior mode attain the efficiency bound of the model with a known regression function, also for Mat\'ern-$5/2$ sample paths. We also characterize small-sample failures of the Laplace approximation as folds of a posterior-mode branch and give a diagnostic. Finally, in a repeated Bayesian optimization study, observation-level tails reduced regret under gross outliers, as did Student-$t$ noise, and no degradation was detected under Gaussian noise.
item.dc:creator: Neelesh S. Upadhye, Rohit Kumar Mani

item.title: Sharp bounds for posterior causal attribution given complete factual records
item.description: arXiv:2611.11307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrospective causal attribution evaluates whether altering an earlier event would have prevented an observed outcome. Observational data determine marginal potential-response probabilities at fixed inputs while leaving cross-world joint distributions unspecified. Conditional on a complete factual record in a finite Markovian structural causal model, independence across mechanisms is preserved and each unobserved conditional response distribution is restricted to a capped probability simplex. Every collection of conditional distributions satisfying these local bounds is jointly attainable within a single compatible structural causal model. Optimizing the counterfactual expectation over the resulting product domain yields sharp attribution bounds for multistage interventions and mediated effects, and compatible response-vector polytopes extend these bounds to structural response restrictions. Exact algorithms for causal chains and general directed acyclic graphs, consistent plug-in endpoint estimators, and finite-sample and asymptotic confidence intervals are developed and illustrated using synthetic reactor experiments and health survey data.
item.dc:creator: Liyao Zhou, Xinwei Sun

item.title: Causal discernment and the direction of clinical research
item.description: arXiv:2611.11311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A clinical trial can establish an intervention's effects while leaving their causal pathways unresolved. We call causal discernment the practice of identifying explanations that fit the evidence but imply different decisions or research directions, and seeking studies that distinguish them. METHOD: We combine causal graphs and prose around four questions: delivery of the intended target change, routes of benefit and harm, stability of causal relations across regimes, and whether unresolved pathways could change the decision. With quantitative assumptions, graphs support plausible reasoning by showing which findings could distinguish explanations even when effects are not identified. Prose specifies clinical meaning, effect size and timing, and supporting evidence. We use conceptual analysis, hypothetical calculations, CAST and lipid-lowering therapy. SUBSTANTIVE RESULTS: Concordant coronary associations for HMGCR and PCSK9 perturbations support LDL mediation over target-specific explanations predicting unequal effects per unit of LDL reduction, but leave a shared receptor pathway possible. Diabetes associations leave LDL lowering, receptor-mediated uptake and weight gain as possible explanations. An illustrative causal record specifies a genetic comparison and assumptions under which it could distinguish them. CONCLUSION: The causal record formalises the reasoning behind the choice of the next study by making competing explanations, evidence and assumptions explicit and stating what each design could resolve. Prepared before a design or recommendation is adopted, it enables scrutiny of that reasoning and interpretation of results in relation to the stated explanations. Its added value over ordinary rationale review remains to be assessed.
item.dc:creator: Carlo Berzuini, Luisa Bernardinelli

item.title: ZIO: Order-Based Structure Learning for Zero-Inflated Count Data under Data Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2611.11448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a structure learning method for directed acyclic graph (DAG) models of zero-inflated multivariate count data. Although causal structure learning with zero-inflated Poisson models is identifiable, existing algorithms rely on local search over the DAG space, leading to poor scalability and a tendency to converge to suboptimal solutions. To address these limitations, we develop a novel order-based scoring framework that searches over variable orderings rather than directly over DAGs. Building on this framework, we further extend the method to multiple heterogeneous datasets by identifying a shared variable ordering while allowing each dataset to have its own edge set. We implement a stochastic hill climbing algorithm with a random-to-random (R2R) proposal operator to efficiently explore the ordering space. Simulation studies show competitive performance against existing methods and improved graph estimation accuracy as more heterogeneous datasets are jointly analyzed under a shared causal ordering. We apply the method to single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from a major depressive disorder study.
item.dc:creator: Fariha Taskin, Junsouk Choi, Hyunwoong Chang

item.title: Model-assisted semi-supervised estimation of the Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.11456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study semi-supervised estimation of the full-lifetime Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring using finite covariate-only samples from two populations. A model-assisted estimator is constructed by adjusting censored pair comparisons with differences between labeled and auxiliary feature means. Resource weights minimize first-order variance within the working projection class. Under joint independent censoring and regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality through a four-pool influence representation that accounts for censoring distributions estimated from the same labeled records. Consistent variance estimation from all four sample pools yields Wald confidence intervals. The efficiency analysis relates variance reduction to projected comparison signals and auxiliary sample sizes and characterizes the gap to the semiparametric bound. A fixed-horizon extension accommodates half-weighted ties and the terminal mass induced by capping follow-up. Simulations show increasing precision gains with auxiliary sample size under moderate or strong projected signals, with finite-sample losses in some settings with zero or weak projected signals. A five-year Rotterdam breast-cancer comparison illustrates precision gains and variability across label allocations when auxiliary samples are formed by controlled outcome withholding.
item.dc:creator: Hengyao Xu, Tao Tan

item.title: Causal Machine Learning for Multilevel Studies with Unmeasured Cluster-Level Covariates via Variational Autoencoders
item.description: arXiv:2611.11483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unmeasured confounders are a key obstacle to accurately estimating treatment effects in observational studies, and in multilevel data, they often arise at the cluster level. Flexible machine learning methods cannot directly resolve such unmeasured confounding. To address this, we propose the variational autoencoder-augmented R-learner (VAE-R), which leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to infer unmeasured cluster-level covariates from the within-cluster dependence of outcome and treatment residuals, and uses the resulting adjustments to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and the average treatment effect (ATE). The VAE decoder is specified through an offset likelihood so that the latent variables capture only the cluster-level variation left unexplained by measured covariates. VAE-R accommodates unmeasured cluster-level confounders in observational studies and unmeasured cluster-level predictors of the outcome in multisite randomized trials. We also provide data-driven strategies for selecting the two hyperparameters of the VAE, the latent dimension size and the Kullback-Leibler weight. Our simulation study shows that VAE-R nearly eliminates the bias of the ordinary R-learner's CATE and ATE estimates in multilevel observational data and improves their precision in multisite randomized trials. Finally, we illustrate VAE-R with two datasets, one from a multilevel observational study and the other from a multisite randomized trial.
item.dc:creator: Youmi Suk, Yuxuan Li

item.title: Graph-regularized synthetic control for spatial panels with post-only treated locations
item.description: arXiv:2611.11496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial policy panels can contain treated locations that are observed only after an intervention and therefore have no pre-treatment outcome history. Without a pre-treatment trajectory to match, choosing donor weights for such post-only locations requires an additional source of information. We propose Graph-SCM, which estimates donor weights jointly across treated locations and encourages geographically neighboring locations to use similar donor combinations. GeoEco-SCM keeps the same geographic graph but adjusts the strength of its existing edges using pre-treatment economic similarity. Both methods handle complete, partial, and absent histories within one convex weight-estimation problem. Monte Carlo experiments compare them with covariate-balanced synthetic controls, equally weighted donor averages, ordinary synthetic control where estimable, and nonseparable spatio-temporal imputation and direct prediction. No method dominates. Graph-based borrowing improves on covariate balancing in several settings, but a selective-coverage design favors covariate balancing. Economic adjustment helps when geography alone misses relevant donor relationships. The results support graph regularization as a way to extend synthetic-control coverage when connected locations share similar donor representations, with its usefulness depending on the structure of the available information.
item.dc:creator: Hajime Seya, Ryosei Moriwaki, Daisuke Murakami

item.title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.11667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.
item.dc:creator: Chang Deng, Inbeom Lee, Bryon Aragam

item.title: ATHOS: Agreement-based Testing of Hypotheses in Overlapping Subgroups
item.description: arXiv:2611.11676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study confirmation of treatment benefit in a prespecified family of overlapping subgroups of a randomized trial. Maximum-statistic procedures exploit the correlation between subgroups' statistics, but calibration decides what they protect. Re-randomization controls error exactly when treatment has no effect, but not when only an average effect is zero, whereas a multiplier bootstrap protects average effects only asymptotically. Our first result characterizes when re-randomization alone protects average effects. It reverses the arms' weights in the statistics' covariance, so with unequal allocation and heterogeneous effects it can overstate their correlations; in one such family of 50 subgroups, its limiting familywise error is 0.064 at nominal 0.025. We propose a step-down procedure called ATHOS, short for agreement-based testing of hypotheses in overlapping subgroups, which confirms a subgroup only when both calibrations reject it. Given assignments exchangeable within strata, ATHOS controls familywise error exactly when treatment has no effect and, under complete randomization, asymptotically for average effects, even in large families. Our second result shows that requiring agreement costs no first-order local power in balanced trials. In a null simulation with 200 patients and 1,497 subgroups, the bootstrap step-down alone made false claims in 40% of trials and ATHOS in 2.6%. In two comparisons in an HIV trial, ATHOS confirmed 188 and 73 subgroups and Holm's procedure 179 and 62.
item.dc:creator: Xiao Wang

item.title: Optimal Radial Weighting for Robust Mutual Fund Selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.11762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying skilled mutual funds requires methods that distinguish positive alphas from sampling variation when many funds are evaluated simultaneously. Heavy-tailed returns and dependence across funds complicate this task. We propose a robust selection procedure based on radially weighted alpha estimation in linear factor pricing models. The method uses both the directions and lengths of standardized residuals, estimates marginal scales from pairwise residual differences, and accounts for the estimation of factor loadings. Within the proposed class, inverse-norm weighting minimizes the asymptotic variance of the alpha estimators and maximizes the local asymptotic power of individual tests at a common significance level. For radial weights fixed conditional on the factor design, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control under elliptically symmetric errors and show that the proportion of sufficiently strong positive-alpha funds selected tends to one. The theory accommodates comparable cross-sectional and time-series dimensions and nonvanishing alphas. We also develop a smoothed implementation and assess its finite-sample properties. Simulations show higher true discovery proportions than least-squares and spatial-sign methods under heavy-tailed distributions and improved numerical stability from smoothing. An application to U.S. equity mutual funds examines the subsequent performance of portfolios formed from the selected funds.
item.dc:creator: Ping Zhao, Qianya Sun, Long Feng

item.title: Distribution-Free Symmetry Detection in Multi-Reference Alignment at Low SNR
item.description: arXiv:2611.11872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetry can reveal the structure of a signal, but detecting it becomes difficult when observations are noisy and randomly transformed. We study how to infer symmetry directly from multi-reference alignment data with additive isotropic Gaussian noise of known variance, without aligning the observations or knowing how the transformations were sampled. For cyclic symmetry, we identify a simple statistical signature that yields tests with exact finite-sample error guarantees. We demonstrate their performance even at very low signal-to-noise ratios. Dihedral symmetry presents a deeper challenge: we show that, for some signals, invariant moments below a sharp order threshold cannot distinguish reflectional from purely rotational symmetry. For generic signals, however, this distinction emerges much earlier. We use these insights to develop tests for dihedral symmetry with asymptotic error control under explicit nondegeneracy conditions. Together, the results clarify what we can learn about symmetry from noisy, unaligned data and suggest a path toward symmetry inference in cryo-EM.
item.dc:creator: Nir Sharon, Sheng Xu

item.title: Semiparametric causal mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials with post-treatment confounding
item.description: arXiv:2611.11903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal mediation analysis of cluster-randomized trials can reveal how interventions affect outcomes through individual and spillover pathways. Most existing methods target natural mediation effects under assumptions that exclude treatment-induced mediator--outcome confounding. We develop a semiparametric framework for interventional mediation effects that accommodates such confounding and within-cluster interference without requiring cross-world independence assumptions. We identify cluster-average and individual-average direct and indirect effects and decompose the indirect effect into individual and spillover components, distinguishing pathways through an individual's own mediator and those of other cluster members. These contrasts evaluate hypothetical interventions on the joint mediator distribution and can differ from treatment effects carried through individual causal pathways represented by natural effects, thereby providing an intervention-oriented perspective that complements natural effects. We derive efficient influence functions to construct estimators using cluster-level cross-fitting, characterize their multiple-robustness properties, and establish conditions for asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency. To facilitate implementation, we develop a lower-dimensional reparameterization that reduces the need for multivariate density estimation and integration and allows nuisance functions to be estimated using parametric models or machine learning. Simulation studies evaluate finite-sample performance, and an application to a cluster-randomized trial of cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain illustrates the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Daeyoung Ham, Chao Cheng, Fan Li

item.title: Characterizing Underrepresentation when Generalizing Causal Survival Estimates
item.description: arXiv:2611.11923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized trial findings are routinely generalized to broader target populations to inform decisions in medicine and public policy. When the trial sample is misaligned with the target population, generalized effect estimates can yield suboptimal decisions. We characterize the target subgroups that are underrepresented in the trial cohort in time-to-event settings. Here, underrepresentation arises in two distinct ways: baseline underrepresentation, when a subgroup's covariate profile is rare in the trial relative to the target, and time-varying underrepresentation, when differential censoring erodes a subgroup over follow-up. Existing diagnostics either conflate these mechanisms or apply only to the baseline case. We show that the asymptotic variance of the efficient generalizability estimator admits a decomposition in which only two terms can diverge as representation weakens: a sampling-weight term capturing baseline misalignment and a censoring-weight term capturing differential loss to follow-up. Underrepresented subgroups are therefore those with imprecise generalized estimates, and the larger of the two terms gives the responsible channel. We use this decomposition in TRACE (Temporal Rashomon Analysis of CEnsored data), which combines a self-normalized variance objective with a tree-based search to localize underrepresented subgroups, attribute each to baseline mismatch or censoring, and find the follow-up intervals where censoring drives the variance inflation. We solve the joint problem with a parametric dynamic program nested inside a Rashomon ensemble of near-optimal trees. In synthetic benchmarks, TRACE recovers the planted underrepresented regions. In a case study generalizing the National Job Training Partnership Act (JTPA) Study to U.S. JTPA-eligible adults, restricting to reliably generalizable subgroups narrows the 95% confidence interval for the refined estimand by 60%.
item.dc:creator: Bolun Liu, Sean McGrath, Yiren Hou, Elizabeth A. Stuart, Harsh Parikh

item.title: A Semiparametric Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model with a Nonparametric Count Distribution for Seizure Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.11928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Functional count data arise when recurrent events are recorded repeatedly over time and scientific interest centers on how event rates evolve over time and across experimental conditions. Standard mixed effects models for counts have interpretable mean structures but require a parametric conditional distribution, which can be restrictive in the presence of overdispersion, unusual zero frequencies and heavy tails. To address these challenges, we develop the functional count DPGLM (fcDPGLM), a semiparametric Bayesian mixed model that combines GLM-style regression with a nonparametric count distribution. Parametric condition-specific mean trajectories and subject-specific random effects determine the conditional mean exactly, allowing the interpretation of contrasts as usual, while remaining details of the count distribution are learned nonparametrically from the data. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models are recovered as limiting cases. A gamma completely random measure representation allows for efficient posterior simulation. In simulations mimicking a rat seizure study, fcDPGLM estimated mean contrasts as accurately as a correctly specified negative-binomial mixed model, and more accurately otherwise, and recovered zero and exceedance probabilities that the parametric models misrepresent. In the seizure study, seizure rates rise and then decline in the early period after induced status epilepticus but remain high and nearly flat in the chronic period, and rats differ substantially. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models estimate similar mean trajectories and period contrasts, but only fcDPGLM matches the observed zero frequency, variance and high-burden days.
item.dc:creator: Entejar Alam, Elizabeth Juarez-Colunga, Marco I. Gonz\'alez, Peter M\"uller

item.title: Conformal Prediction for Multi-Step Forecasting: Conditional Coverage and Sharp Score Calibration Rates
item.description: arXiv:2611.12004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty quantification in prediction is a central problem in statistics and machine learning. Conformal prediction provides a flexible approach to constructing prediction sets with valid marginal coverage under exchangeability. In this paper, we investigate conformal prediction for both one-step and multi-step forecasting from a single stationary time series, addressing temporal dependence and the additional challenges of joint prediction across multiple horizons. We propose a kernel-based framework, called Time series Residual Analysis for Calibration with Kernels (TRACK), for estimating conditional quantiles of residual scores and constructing prediction sets from rolling-window forecasters. The framework accommodates heterogeneous uncertainty across horizons and accounts for dependence induced by rolling estimation, while allowing predictor memory and forecast horizons to grow with the sample size. Our finite-sample bounds quantify how temporal dependence and overlapping score windows affect calibration and coverage. We further derive bounds for conditional quantile estimation and pointwise conditional coverage discrepancy. The guarantees extend to more general predictors that admit an accurate rolling-window approximation. We also derive matching minimax bounds over classes of known score maps, clarifying how overlapping score windows affect calibration accuracy. Experimental results from simulations and applications to wind energy generation and bike sharing demand show that our methods improve regional conditional coverage while maintaining competitive interval widths.
item.dc:creator: Siyuan He, Yuhong Yang

item.title: Zero-inflated generalized linear latent variable models for microbiome compositional data
item.description: arXiv:2611.12163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we incorporate the Dirichlet--multinomial distribution into the generalized linear latent variable model (GLLVM) framework to accommodate high-dimensional, overdispersed compositional count data and capture complex covariation among taxa with a low-rank structure. Advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies have generated large amounts of microbiome count data, stimulating research into their associations with human diseases and traits. Such data are compositional and often highly sparse for various reasons, posing challenges for statistical analysis. Conventional zero-replacement approaches ignore the underlying causes of zeros, further complicating the analysis. We therefore propose a zero-inflated Dirichlet--multinomial latent variable model (ZIDM-LVM). Since the marginal likelihood has no closed-form expression, we develop a variational approximation (VA) approach for efficient parameter estimation. Simulation studies and applications to two microbiome datasets are presented to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Wenqi Tang, Pekka Korhonen, Jenni Niku, Klaus Nordhausen, Sara Taskinen

item.title: Data-Adaptive Subset-Size Selection for Minimum Covariance Determinant Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Subset size determines the balance between robustness and efficiency in minimum covariance determinant estimation. Conventional choices fix this balance before the extent and structure of contamination are known. Reweighting does not remove the influence of the initial subset size. We propose a data-adaptive rule based on ordered squared Mahalanobis distances. It selects the first window maximum, with window width proportional to the sample size. For a minimum covariance determinant subset, the statistic equals the smallest squared distance among excluded observations. For smooth elliptical distributions with small one-point contamination, we characterize the first population window maximum. Under suitable conditions, it is the last retained fraction at which excluding the contaminating point remains optimal. We derive a first-order expansion for this boundary and establish sample localization along the full integer path. Without contamination, the selected fraction tends to one. A fast depth-based implementation reuses one ordering across candidate sizes. Simulations under Gaussian and heavy-tailed sampling show gains over fixed subset sizes, most consistently for scatter estimation. Real data analyses show that the initial subset size affects which observations are retained after reweighting.
item.dc:creator: Chikun Li, Baisuo Jin

item.title: Algorithm-aware Statistical Inference in High-dimensional Estimating Equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.12287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Iterative algorithms are integral to many statistical procedures, whereas sampling uncertainty along their iteration is generally not quantified. We develop simultaneous inference for discrete trajectories generated from high-dimensional estimating equations, with iteration-specific population estimands that preserve algorithmic regularization. Our proposed fixed-Jacobian bootstrap propagates perturbations along the observed trajectory without repeatedly running the original nonlinear algorithm. We establish uniform first-order expansions and bootstrap validity over possibly infinite sets of contrasts and iterations under stability, entropy and moment conditions. Simulations in sparse linear regression, paired Fisher discrimination, and temporal-difference learning demonstrate accurate simultaneous coverage. A micro-randomized trial application illustrates inference for a treatment trajectory with participant-level clustering.
item.dc:creator: Tongyu Li, Alexander Giessing

item.title: TRACE: Adaptive Credibility Reweighting for Robust Bayesian Model Selection with Source Summary Statistics
item.description: arXiv:2611.12352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study focuses on regression estimation and variable selection based on target data, while incorporating information from coefficient estimates obtained in related studies. A weighted combination of these estimates may agree with some target effects but differ from others. We propose Transfer Regression with Adaptive Credibility Estimation (TRACE), a Bayesian method requiring only fitted coefficients and sample sizes from source studies. TRACE learns simplex-constrained source weights shared across variables. Separate latent indicators determine target inclusion and whether each coefficient is guided by the weighted source estimate. We develop an approximate collapsed variational expectation-maximization algorithm with robust source-weight initialization. Under suitable conditions, consistency of variable selection, transfer decisions, and source-weight estimation is established. These results hold at every prespecified fixed iteration in fixed dimension and at global mean-field optima of the exact collapsed variational objective as the dimension grows. Simulations show that TRACE achieves competitive variable-selection performance under different patterns of source heterogeneity. An application to data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression project illustrates its use in cross-tissue gene-expression prediction.
item.dc:creator: Pengfei Chen, Yuehan Yang, Lucy Klinger, Chong You

item.title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series
item.description: arXiv:2611.12368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Series in a macroeconomic panel are almost all correlated with one another, which makes correlation a poor guide to which pairs are directly linked. For example, Treasury rates at different maturities are all highly correlated, yet a short and a long rate may be related only through the rates at maturities between them; similarly, sectors of the economy such as output, employment, prices, and interest rates may be related directly or only through other series. Both are questions about the inverse covariance matrix. Recovering it from quarterly data is difficult: contemporaneous dependence is entangled with temporal dynamics, the innovations remain densely dependent once those dynamics are removed, and the number of series is comparable to the number of quarters observed. We propose VAPOR (Vector Autoregressive Precision factOR), a Bayesian model that estimates vector autoregressive dynamics jointly with a factor-structured innovation precision matrix, inferring the partial correlations directly from the fitted precision rather than imposing a zero pattern. Applied to 100 quarterly FRED-QD series, VAPOR learns from the data that each Treasury rate is directly related only to the rates at adjacent maturities, places all 26 selected dependencies within a single FRED-QD group, and attains the lowest held-out prediction error among the estimators compared.
item.dc:creator: Peter Dunson

item.title: Robust Posterior Projection for Bayesian Inference Under Order Restrictions
item.description: arXiv:2611.12513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In archaeology and geochronology, stratigraphic information constrains the relative chronological order of dated samples. Bayesian chronological models incorporate these constraints either through the prior, or by projecting an unconstrained posterior distribution onto the set of ordered chronologies. Dating measurements may nevertheless appear inconsistent with their stratigraphic position, owing to disturbances that do not justify discarding them. We introduce different robust projection maps based on the Huber loss and characterize the non-uniqueness of the considered maps which justifies a Tikhonov regularization. The robust maps also decompose each sample into a monotone baseline and a spike, which flags questionable samples. We adapt the Sequential Block Merging algorithm for the Huber-type losses, and propose a data-driven heuristic for selecting the hyperparameter on which each loss depends on. Simulation studies and geochronological case studies illustrate the gains in robustness and their limits.
item.dc:creator: Im{\`e}ne Bouafia (CFE), Anne Philippe (LMJL), Guillaume Gu{\'e}rin (GR)

item.title: Graph-Guided Bayesian Factor Analysis: A Fast Integrated EFA-CFA Approach for High-Dimensional Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.12612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Factor analysis has been central to the analysis of high-dimensional biomedical data. However, existing exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis methods face several limitations: less interpretable factor findings, difficulty in identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors, challenges in estimating the covariance among factors, and maximum-likelihood fits that break down when variables outnumber subjects. We propose graph-guided Bayesian factor analysis (gg-BFA) to address these gaps. We first use a Bayesian model to explore and learn the latent graph structure, identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors and how many factors are needed. A dense-subgraph search proposes partitions of the variables into communities, each defining one factor, and a forward stepwise search compares their fractional variational posteriors and stops when the evidence lower bound first decreases. We show that this search recovers the true communities even when the number of variables grows much faster than the sample size. We then develop a confirmatory Bayesian model whose variational posterior of the covariance contracts at the parametric rate up to a logarithmic factor, yielding posterior inference for the factors and their covariance, as well as predictions of missing values. Its four members range from a community mask to several cross-loadings per variable. In five biomedical panels, the complete analysis took under ten minutes each on one GPU, and cross-loadings improved held-out covariance and the prediction of masked measurements. In TCGA Kidney, six of the first eight factors were enriched for known pathways, and 190 of the 210 factor correlations had 95% credible intervals excluding zero. Overall, gg-BFA is computationally fast and provides interpretable factor analysis findings and reliable inference results.
item.dc:creator: Shitao Fan, Lizhen Lin, Zhenyao Ye, Shuo Chen

item.title: Near-Purity Screening and Dominant-Atom Estimation in Softmax Mixtures and Their Ensembles
item.description: arXiv:2611.12647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study near-purity screening and dominant-atom estimation in softmax mixtures, whose components share a common set of category features. A mixture is called $\varepsilon$-pure if one of its mixing weights is at least $1-\varepsilon$. We introduce the Trace of Latent Covariance Criterion ($\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$), a direct estimator of the trace of the covariance matrix of the latent mixing measure, constructed without estimating its atoms or weights, or knowing the number of components. Unlike existing moment-based approaches, our estimator is constructed for the softmax family and does not require knowledge or estimation of the feature distribution. We establish finite-sample guarantees for $\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$, showing that it achieves a parametric convergence rate up to an additive approximation error of order $p^{-1/2}$, without requiring minimum separation between mixture atoms. We also study estimation of the dominant atom in near-pure mixtures by fitting a single softmax component. We prove that the resulting maximum likelihood estimator has an error bound consisting of the usual parametric term and a bias term governed by the weighted distances between the dominant and remaining atoms, revealing adaptation to the geometry of the mixture. Finally, we extend near-purity screening and dominant-atom estimation to ensembles of softmax mixtures with shared atoms and mixture-specific weights. We apply $\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$ separately to each ensemble member to screen for near-purity without knowing the number of components. Under additional assumptions, clustering the resulting dominant-atom estimators yields finite-sample guarantees for estimating the shared atoms. An application to the Million Song Dataset illustrates how the estimated softmax directions reveal interpretable structure in the data.
item.dc:creator: Xin Bing, Florentina Bunea, Marten Wegkamp, Weicheng Wu

item.title: Spatially varying quantile downscaling of summer temperature from atmospheric circulation and long-term trends over peninsular Spain
item.description: arXiv:2611.12677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over recent decades, high temperatures have intensified worldwide, with impacts on human health, ecosystems, and the economy. Understanding their spatial evolution requires accounting for long-term temperature changes and the role of atmospheric circulation. Quantile regression provides a flexible framework for characterizing changes across the temperature distribution, with relevance to extremes. We analyze the spatio-temporal evolution of the 0.50 and 0.95 quantiles of daily maximum temperature during summer (June--August) over peninsular Spain from 1960 to 2023. We develop a Bayesian spatially varying quantile regression model for observations from 40 meteorological stations, using ERA5 geopotential fields at tropospheric levels to characterize atmospheric circulation, together with long-term temporal trends capturing the background climate change signal. The spatially varying coefficients allow the sensitivity of temperature to atmospheric circulation to differ across the region, linking synoptic dynamics with local temperature variability. The model separates changes associated with the dynamical atmospheric state from the long-term thermodynamic warming signal, while allowing their effects to vary across the temperature distribution. Results show that atmospheric circulation and long-term trends provide comparable contributions to the observed warming. Significant increases in median and upper-quantile temperatures are found across much of peninsular Spain, with pronounced heterogeneity across months and space, followed by quantiles
item.dc:creator: Juan Marcen-Gutierrez, Jorge Castillo-Mateo

item.title: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks
item.description: arXiv:2611.12690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. Given an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping, we show that potential outcomes admit a nonparametric decomposition into direct, spillover, and treatment--spillover interaction components. This decomposition provides a common coordinate system for nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric models of finite-population potential outcomes. For a given potential-outcome model, we define two classes of estimands. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as direct and total treatment effects, contrast potential outcomes under fixed treatment--exposure conditions. Expected causal effects (ECEs), such as expected direct and indirect effects, contrast expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy. For both classes, we bound the variance of the canonical Horvitz--Thompson estimator by three terms: a diagonal weight term, a term from overlapping interference neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term. Our upper and lower bounds show that under graph-unaware designs, nonparametric design-unbiased estimation of ACEs can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the interference degree, whereas polynomial growth can suffice for design-aligned ECEs. Under neighborhood interference, we construct graph-aware independent-set designs with variance bounds polynomial in the maximum degree for direct and total treatment effects on every graph, whereas graph cluster randomization can incur worst-case variance exponential in the degree.
item.dc:creator: Vishesh Karwa, Edoardo M. Airoldi, Donald B. Rubin

item.title: Change-point analysis of textual data: a flexible approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.12837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a CUSUM-based change-point procedure for word-frequency vectors that accounts for the variation in the amount of observed textual information over time. Under a multinomial model, we derive the asymptotic null distribution of the proposed statistic, allowing for varying document numbers and lengths. With trimming based on cumulative word counts, the limiting null distribution does not depend on the temporal distribution of textual information. We also consider parametric and nonparametric bootstrap procedures for finite-sample calibration. A simulation study examines their performance under both multinomial sampling and Dirichlet mixtures of multinomial distributions. The results demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach under increasing document intensity and show that resampling entire documents provides more reliable calibration in the presence of document-level heterogeneity. Finally, we apply the procedure, combined with binary segmentation, to 68,542 abstracts from the arXiv category stat.ML spanning 2007-2025, identifying multiple changes in word-usage patterns.
item.dc:creator: Bojana Milo\v{s}evi\'c, Luka Perovi\'c

item.title: Measuring Public Institutions and their Agents: Disparities and Agreement, with Application to Asylum Decisions in the U.S. Immigration Courts
item.description: arXiv:2611.10308v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public institutions derive their legitimacy from the professionalism and impartiality of their agents. In order to maintain standards of conduct, the performance of an agent is often compared to the performance of her peers. But public institutions typically assign agents to different tasks, and as a result, naive comparisons may reflect the difficulty of the assignment and not an agent's performance. To address this concern, we develop measures of disparity and agreement that compare an agent's performance with the potential performance of randomly selected peers who could have been assigned the same set of tasks. We then give realistic conditions under which disparity is identified from the marginal distribution of each agent's actions. We also show how agreement, which is generally unidentified when agents are assigned to different tasks, can be bounded or estimated under sensitivity assumptions about the dependence between potential outcomes. Finally, we use a nonparametric Bayesian model to examine applications for asylum filed between 2007 and 2014 in the widely studied and often maligned U.S. immigration courts. Our results do not support the picture of widespread partiality asserted in previous empirical work. At both the judge and court level, we find limited disparity and substantial potential agreement.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Auerbach, Michael E. Sobel

item.title: Divide-and-Conquer is Tail- and Anomaly-Robust: Factor Model Estimation Without Moment Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.10358v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study robust estimation of elliptical factor models with abnormal observations and without requiring the existence of any positive moments. In particular, a divide-and-conquer (DC) estimator averages orthogonal projectors onto the full column spaces of small data blocks, and we rigorously establish its probability bound that allows weak and heterogeneous factors. The derived convergence rate is comparable to that of classical principal component estimators, up to the proportion of anomalies. Building on our DC estimator, we propose a split-sample tail- and anomaly-robust (STAR) estimator for the factor number using sample medians of successive projected coordinate ratios, which is shown consistent under mild conditions. Subsequent factor and common component estimation is also discussed, with the rates of convergence spelled out. Remarkably, given an upper bound on the true factor number, our suite of procedures are free from tuning, require no tail-dependent truncation threshold nor solving an optimization problem, admit parallel block computations, and hence has the same computational complexity as the classical principal component methods. Extensive experiments corroborate our theoretical findings, where DC and STAR are comparable and often outperform state-of-the-art competitors. We also illustrate our methods on a portfolio return dataset.
item.dc:creator: Zetai Cen, Han Yan, Haeran Cho

item.title: Panel Local Projections with Missing Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.10372v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A panel local projection can remain identified even when missing data leave no complete regression case. We recover the projection over specified dates by combining factor-based conditional means with idiosyncratic covariances from observed pairs. Under strong factors in the auxiliary panel, sufficient factor variation at observed dates and enough observations of the required pairs, a second-order expansion yields bias-corrected moments and a joint score for inference. The localized multiplier bootstrap provides pointwise confidence intervals and simultaneous bands under additional dependence restrictions. We revisit the investment response to geopolitical risk studied by Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) with a larger quarterly firm sample and extend the analysis to monthly projections of trailing-three-month investment intensity. In the monthly analysis, the six-month response difference between high- and low-exposure firms becomes more negative as firms with incomplete histories enter the sample.
item.dc:creator: Yubo Tao

item.title: Matchability-Aware Conformal Prediction for Open-Ended Language Model Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10738v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers. We propose CAELUM, a framework that builds semantic prediction sets while separating aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. CAELUM samples answers using an ensemble of clarification prompts, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and estimates the aleatoric and epistemic components via kernel-based von Neumann entropy before calibrating nonconformity scores with split conformal prediction. We use a weight $w_\lambda(x)=1+U_{\mathrm{ale}}(x)+\lambda\,U_{\mathrm{epi}}(x)$ to control for the contribution of the epistemic uncertainty of each instance and fit a coefficient $\lambda^\star$ to minimize prediction set size. When the objective is nonflat and selection is stable across splits, $\lambda^\star$ could be a diagnostic, where large values may indicate epistemic dominance (retrieve, abstain) and $\lambda^\star\to 0$ aleatoric dominance (clarify). For individual queries, a log ratio $R(x)$ compares the weighted epistemic component with the aleatoric component. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the coverage is capped by matchability, the fraction of items whose reference answer appears in any sampled cluster. Empirically, this matchability can be predicted from the original question features using a lightweight classifier. We use those predictions to define a stratum and derive a conformal coverage bound within it. Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations (4-32B), mean coverage is 0.74 in the learned stratum versus 0.65 overall, averaged over the 78 evaluations using the learned classifier. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/caelum/
item.dc:creator: Ilia Azizi

item.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2611.10787v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs). Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help determine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate's 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement.
item.dc:creator: Zihe Gao, Zhengling Qi, Yifan Cui

item.title: Bayesian Wombling for Tracking Invasive Species
item.description: arXiv:2611.10871v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper develops Bayesian wombling, or boundary analysis for tracking invasive species. We focus on three invasive species of concern in North America: Lycorma delicatula, Adelges tsugae, and Microstegium vimineum. We aim to demonstrate the applicability of wombling for supporting invasive pest management activities. In spatial science wombling is used widely to track regions of rapid change within the spatial reference domain. We use Gaussian process models for point-referenced spatial data followed by predictive inference on rates of change over curves using line integrals. We extend the wombling model based Bayesian inference framework to feature simple analytic forms that avoid high dimensional quadrature while offering uncertainty quantification over curvilinear spatial boundaries.
item.dc:creator: Aritra Halder, Joseph R. Stinziano, Joshua Persi

item.title: Sequential anomaly identification with sampling constraints for composite hypotheses
item.description: arXiv:2611.10921v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the problem of sequential anomaly identification with sampling constraints, where multiple independent data sources are observed over time, but only a limited subset can be sampled at each instant. The objective is to identify the anomalous sources while controlling the probabilities of at least one false alarm and at least one missed detection below prescribed levels. An identification policy must jointly determine when to stop sampling, which sources to declare anomalous, and how to allocate observations across sources under the sampling constraints. We seek policies that minimize the expected time to decision to a first-order asymptotic approximation as the error probabilities vanish. The observations from each source follow an unknown density belonging to one of two disjoint sets, corresponding to regular and anomalous behavior. Focusing on a nonparametric framework, which allows greater flexibility in modeling regular and anomalous statistical behavior, we establish general conditions for asymptotic optimality and provide a unified characterization of asymptotically optimal policies for composite hypothesis testing under sampling constraints. Simulation results illustrate the performance of the proposed policies, and the robustness of the nonparametric framework.
item.dc:creator: Aristomenis Tsopelakos, Georgios Fellouris, Olgica Milenkovic

item.title: Analysis increments for model bias diagnosis and correction: Theoretical foundations
item.description: arXiv:2611.11162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A common method for diagnosing and correcting model bias in weather and climate prediction is based on analysis increments: the difference between the analysis and the forecast at each data assimilation cycle. Their time average is used to estimate and correct the bias, and machine learning is increasingly used to map the forecast state to the increments, giving a state-dependent correction. Despite its widespread use, the method lacks theoretical foundations. We first analyse a Kalman filter whose forecast model has a constant bias. We show what the averaged increment measures, and prove that iterating the correction removes all of the bias seen through the observations; for linear dynamics, no method can identify the rest. We then extend the analysis to state-dependent biases. For linear dynamics, each increment records the model error over the filter's memory, as seen through the observations. We use this to determine what the increments measure when averaged over a long period, averaged over periods with similar slowly varying conditions, and used without averaging, as in machine-learned corrections. Numerical experiments confirm the theory for a linear model and suggest that its main conclusions carry over to the nonlinear Lorenz '96 model, including for a correction learned by a neural network.
item.dc:creator: Eviatar Bach

item.title: Zero Replacement and Latent Profiles in Short Media Diaries: Checking Recording Status Before User Segmentation
