item.description: arXiv:2611.11274v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Short media diaries contain many zeros because many activities go unrecorded during the observation period. Log-ratio analysis of time allocation requires these zeros to be replaced with small positive values; as a result, all respondents who did not record an activity receive nearly the same value. We examined how such zero replacement affects classification in latent profile analysis and propose checks to perform before profiles are interpreted. Three-day diaries of 8,089 adults from the 2025 Korea Media Panel Survey were converted into nine-part time-use compositions. Gaming was not recorded by 88.9% of the respondents, and in every model with two to eight profiles and a covariance matrix held equal across profiles, respondents who recorded gaming and those who did not were classified into different profiles. Even when the replacement value equaled the minimum recording unit (5 min/day), the two-profile classification largely matched gaming recording status, and the two groups separated more sharply as the replacement value decreased, until the separation was complete. Before naming profiles, researchers should therefore check the proportion of respondents who did not record each activity and its replacement value, the same proportion within each profile, and the distribution of usage time among those who recorded the activity.
item.dc:creator: Eunjeong Song, Sehee Hong

item.title: Tail behaviour of infimum of Gaussian processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.11285v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the upper tail of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$, where $X$ is a centred Gaussian process (GP) with continuous sample paths on a nonempty compact metric space $\mathcal T$. As suggested by the findings of [1], the exponential rate is governed by an optimal-measure problem, while the exact prefactor depends on the local geometry of the corresponding contact set. In the full-contact regime, we strengthen the known Gumbel max-domain of attraction property of the distribution of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$ by establishing the von Mises condition. For fractional Brownian motion on $[a,b]$, $0<a<b$, with Hurst index $H\in(0,1/2)$, we also determine the order of the logarithmic correction to the leading Gaussian exponential. For finite contact sets, we distinguish dominated, smooth-critical, and rough-critical regimes and derive exact asymptotics of $P\{\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)>u\}$ as $u\to\infty$ under suitable local assumptions. We illustrate our findings with examples including fractional Brownian motion and the fractional Brownian sheet.
item.dc:creator: K. Debicki, E. Hashorva, S. Novikov

item.title: Does Predictive Performance Translate to Causal Performance? Evaluating tabular foundation models as nuisance learners for causal effect estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.11381v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) achieve strong predictive performance, but their value for causal inference is unclear. We evaluated whether PFNs, which predict through in-context learning, could match or outperform conventional nuisance learners in supporting accurate causal estimation and reliable uncertainty quantification (inference). Learners modeled propensity scores and outcome regressions within doubly robust estimators of average causal effects, with and without cross-fitting, across synthetic and semi-synthetic settings with varying confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity. Under simple parametric data-generating processes, the PFNs were competitive with correctly specified parametric regressions and ensembles containing them. In more complex settings, they outperformed all conventional learners evaluated, including richly specified Super Learner ensembles, for both accuracy and uncertainty quantification. As sample size increased, only the two PFN models (TabPFN and Mitra) consistently approached nominal confidence interval coverage, whereas under-coverage persisted for conventional learners. In some settings, PFNs achieved near-nominal coverage and well-calibrated standard errors even without cross-fitting. At the smallest sample size (n=200) and in the higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs and other flexible learners exhibited poor coverage without cross-fitting. For PFNs, this appeared to be driven by propensity score overfitting consistent with in-sample memorization of treatment labels. These findings highlight the promise of prior-data fitted networks as in-context nuisance learners for causal estimation, while underscoring the need for further evaluation in challenging settings.
item.dc:creator: Andrew R Weckstein, Issa J Dahabreh, Marinka Zitnik, Sonia Hern\'andez-D\'iaz, Sebastian Schneeweiss

item.title: Uniform inference for $U$-statistics of exchangeable arrays under degeneracy
item.description: arXiv:2611.11388v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many $U$-statistics of row-column exchangeable arrays become degenerate at natural null hypotheses: their convergence rates change and their limiting laws may or may not remain Gaussian. We establish conditions under which inference based on the classical unbiased variance estimator is uniformly valid across these changes, without knowledge of the degeneracy order. It is known that $U$-statistics can be decomposed into orthogonal projections indexed by bipartite graphs. Under uniform fourth-moment assumptions, we establish that the standardized statistic is asymptotically Gaussian and the classical unbiased variance estimator is ratio-consistent, as long as a certain measure of concentration for projections indexed by disconnected graphs tends to zero. Under compactness of the normalized projections, both properties hold if and only if the proportion of variance contributed by disconnected graphs tends to zero. The necessity of this condition follows from a general limit theorem for these $U$-statistics, in which each graph contributes to a Wiener chaos of order equal to its number of connected components. We note that the row-column jackknife variance estimator, although nonnegative, does not generally give a studentized statistic with a standard normal limit in degenerate regimes. We illustrate our theory with an application to estimation and testing based on a distance from product form, exhibiting Gaussian and non-Gaussian limits at various rates depending on the model. We also propose a conservative inference procedure that does not require a Gaussian limit, valid under additional moment and projection conditions.
item.dc:creator: T\^am LeMinh

item.title: Identifiable alignment of unpaired representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.11460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. We show that this symmetry breaking holds generically. Identifiability makes the alignment coupling the unique optimum of Gromov--Wasserstein and of its weighted combinations with a linear program. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.
item.dc:creator: Stas Syrota, Albert Lopez I Serrano, Johanne Franck, S{\o}ren Hauberg

item.title: The Dark Matter of Clinical Data: An Identification Limit on Disentangling Physiology from Care Process in electronic health records
item.description: arXiv:2611.11726v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Representations learned from electronic health record (EHR) data encode patient physiology together with the clinical process that decides what is measured, when, and for whom. We formalize the data-generating process with latent physiology, ordering intent, laboratory values that exist only when measured, a learned representation, and clinical environments, and analyze two strategies for undoing this entanglement. First, no division of the information carried by laboratory "value" and "ordering" channels is identified from a single dataset: when ordering depends on the analyte, its distribution among untested patients is not recoverable, and a sentinel code for the undefined recorded value makes it carry all the entropy of the ordering indicator, fixing partial information decomposition (PID) for every redundancy measure satisfying the Williams-Beer axioms and invariant under injective re-encoding. Second, cross-site invariance of representation-conditional outcomes is a falsifiable implication of biological invariance taken jointly with exclusion and representation-sufficiency conditions, but not an identification strategy: we construct observationally equivalent models that disagree about biological invariance, whether the invariance test fails or passes. For binary physiology this happens exactly when case mix differs, the representation is lossy, and physiology affects the outcome. A worked example yields a 9.6-percentage-point cross-site gap under an unchanged biological mechanism. Tests performed for every patient remove the ordering gate, and measured tests can restore identification: biological invariance is identified when a test exactly summarizes outcome-relevant physiology, or, for binary physiology, when two tests with independent errors are available at sites with different case mix. Cross-site analyses should be reported as tests of a stated joint hypothesis.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Shahin, Krittaphas Chaisutyakorn, Dimitrios Proios, David Restrepo, Vishala Mishra, Boya Zhang, Aadarsh Sivaraman, Sparsh Roy, Benet Fit\'e Abril, Tina Yen-Ting Chen, Hyunjung Gloria Kwak, Andre Kurepa Waschka, Vinayak Mathur, Leo Anthony Celi

item.title: On the robustness of locally D-optimal designs under parameter uncertainty in single-factor generalized linear models
item.description: arXiv:2611.11785v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local and Bayesian approaches to optimal experimental design specify information about the regression parameters through a nominal value and a prior distribution, respectively. A practical question is whether accounting for parameter uncertainty justifies replacing a locally optimal design. We investigate when locally D-optimal designs remain Bayesian D-optimal in single-factor Poisson, gamma and logistic regression on the unit interval. Analytical arguments and numerical comparisons under normal and uniform slope priors examine how prior form and dispersion affect the optimal support and the Bayesian D-efficiency of retaining a local design.
item.dc:creator: Osama Idais

item.title: An iterated-logarithm price of anytime validity for log-optimal e-processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.11874v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Log-optimal e-variables at fixed horizons, also called num\'eraires, have been conjectured to ``almost'' form an e-process for exponential-family null hypotheses. A related open question is whether an e-process can attain the optimal e-power at every horizon up to a bounded loss. Given a final horizon, we study the minimax regret of e-processes relative to the num\'eraires at all times up to it. For the Gaussian location null and the composite alternative of Gaussian distributions with a smaller variance and an unknown location, we show that the minimax regret in the worst case over the location grows like the iterated logarithm of the final horizon. A single e-process attains this rate at every horizon. This growth answers the question negatively. It also refutes the conjecture if ``almost'' means a regret bounded uniformly over horizons. For this Gaussian location problem, we thus exhibit the frontier precisely: the minimax regret is bounded if and only if the alternatives have at least the variance of the null.
item.dc:creator: Adrien Corenflos

item.title: A weighted edge-count two-sample test for multivariate and object data
item.description: arXiv:1604.06515v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-sample tests for multivariate data and non-Euclidean data are widely used in many fields. Parametric tests are mostly restrained to certain types of data that meets the assumptions of the parametric models. In this paper, we study a nonparametric testing procedure that utilizes graphs representing the similarity among observations. It can be applied to any data types as long as an informative similarity measure on the sample space can be defined. The classic test based on a similarity graph has a problem when the two sample sizes are different. We solve the problem by applying appropriate weights to different components of the classic test statistic. The new test exhibits substantial power gains in simulation studies. Its asymptotic permutation null distribution is derived and shown to work well under finite samples, facilitating its application to large datasets. The new test is illustrated through an analysis on a real dataset of network data.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of the American Statistical Association, 113(523), 1146-1155, 2018
item.dc:creator: Hao Chen, Xu Chen, Yi Su

item.title: MML Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2209.14559v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is perhaps the most widely used method for data dimensionality reduction. A key question in PCA is deciding how many components to retain. This manuscript describes a new approach to automatically selecting the number of principal components based on the Bayesian minimum message length method of inductive inference. We derive new estimates of the isotropic residual variance and loadings, and establish their bias and asymptotic distributions. For moderate latent dimensions, the residual variance estimate improves on maximum likelihood, and the implied eigenvalue shrinkage approaches the Stein-optimal shrinkage for strong signals.
item.dc:creator: Enes Makalic, Daniel F. Schmidt

item.title: Personalized Pricing with Invalid Instrumental Variables: Identification, Estimation, and Policy Learning
item.description: arXiv:2302.12670v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pricing based on individual customer characteristics is widely used to maximize sellers' revenues. We study how a firm can learn such a personalized pricing policy from historical transactions when unobserved factors affect both the prices it charged and the revenue it earned. Standard instrumental variable (IV) methods either focus on a discrete treatment space or require that the IV affect revenue only through price. This exclusion restriction is difficult to justify in pricing, where the most natural candidate IVs are price-setting levers that may also affect revenue directly. We propose PRINT (Personalized pRicing using Invalid iNsTrumental variables), a policy learning method for continuous prices that uses such candidate IVs. Relying on structural models of revenue and price, we show that the optimal pricing policy can be identified with invalid IV that shifts higher moments of historical prices, when the unobserved factors that drive customers' price sensitivity are separated from those used by the historical pricing rule. Based on this identification, which leads to conditional moment restrictions with generalized residual functions, we construct an adversarial min-max estimator that accommodates flexible machine learning models and establish regret bounds for the learned pricing policy. Simulation studies and an application to a U.S. online auto lender illustrate the method's performance. Our results give a principled way to learn personalized prices from observational data using imperfect price-setting levers, and clarify when doing so is justified.
item.dc:creator: Rui Miao, Zhengling Qi, Cong Shi, Lin Lin

item.title: Rank-Transformed Dissimilarity Profiles for High-Dimensional Classification
item.description: arXiv:2306.15199v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite advances in representation learning, high-dimensional classification remains challenging in low-sample-size regimes, where the dominant signal may vary across applications and labeled data are often limited. We propose a dissimilarity-profiling classification framework that represents each observation by its class-wise dissimilarity profile, transforming the original feature space into a low-dimensional representation that summarizes how the observation relates to each class. The key idea is to turn an effect of the curse of dimensionality into signal: high-dimensional geometry can induce systematic within-class and between-class dissimilarity patterns under location, scale, or other distributional changes, and these patterns are captured by the class-wise profiles. Building on this representation, we introduce a rank-transformed algorithm that converts dissimilarities into class-wise rank profiles. The proposed method delivers competitive or improved performance relative to commonly used classifiers on two-class, multi-class, network, and real high-dimensional low-sample-size datasets. To clarify the underlying mechanism, we characterize the mean and covariance of a distance-based surrogate, showing how location, scale, and higher-order distributional features enter the profile representation. Contamination experiments show that the rank transformation can improve robustness. The same profile construction applies to non-Euclidean data whenever pairwise dissimilarities can be computed.
item.dc:creator: Xiangbo Mo, Hao Chen

item.title: Spatial fusion of DHS and MICS surveys with jittered and geomasked locations
item.description: arXiv:2405.04928v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In low- and middle-income countries, survey data is a key data source for public health monitoring. Not accounting for the anonymization applied to the GPS locations in these surveys may lead to bias, and in turn sub-optimal public health decision-making and outcomes. We propose a spatial fusion model to account both for jittering (a form of random perturbation of GPS coordinates) and geomasking (reporting only the name of the area containing the true GPS coordinates). This allows us to combine data from surveys with different kinds of positional uncertainty, reduce bias, and give more precise estimates. We use this approach to estimate women's secondary education completion through a fusion model using both the 2018 Nigeria demographic and health survey (DHS), with jittered point locations, and the 2016 Nigeria multiple indicator cluster (MICS) survey, with geomasked locations. We show that accounting for the positional uncertainty in the surveys and accounting for both DHS and MICS surveys simultaneously can reduce bias while improving precision in parameter estimates and predictions via a simulation study and validation at cluster and areal levels. We recommend the proposed approach particularly in cases where the modeler wishes to model DHS and MICS surveys jointly, where continuously varying spatial covariates are used, and where local targeted spatial estimates are desired.
item.dc:creator: John Paige, Geir-Arne Fuglstad, Andrea Riebler

item.title: Simulation Studies For Goodness-of-Fit and Two-Sample Methods For Univariate Data
item.description: arXiv:2411.05839v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the results of a large number of simulation studies regarding the power of various goodness-of-fit as well as nonparametric two-sample tests for univariate data. This includes both continuous and discrete data. In general no single method can be relied upon to provide good power, any one method may be quite good for some combination of null hypothesis and alternative and may fail badly for another. Based on the results of these studies we propose a fairly small number of methods chosen such that for any of the case studies included here at least one of the methods has good power. The studies were carried out using the R packages R2sample and Rgof, available from CRAN.
item.dc:creator: Wolfgang Rolke

item.title: High-Dimensional Markov-Switching Ordinary Differential Processes
item.description: arXiv:2501.00087v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complex systems often evolve in continuous time but are observed only at discrete time points with measurement noise. When the interactions can change across unobserved states, recovering both the state transitions and the differential equations is important for mechanistic insight and for identifying time-varying directed graphs. However, this recovery is challenging in high dimensions. In this paper, we study estimation and graph recovery for high-dimensional Markov-switching ordinary differential equation models from noisy discrete observations. We model the switching between states by a latent continuous-time Markov chain, and within each state the drift is a sparse additive function with unknown nonlinear components. We approximate each component by a finite basis expansion and estimate the parameters under group sparsity. Our procedure estimates the latent trajectories by wavelet smoothing and then runs a penalized surrogate expectation-maximization algorithm. Under stationarity and geometric $\beta$-mixing, given a sufficiently accurate estimated trajectory and other local regularity conditions, we show that the algorithm converges geometrically to a neighborhood of the true parameters. Finally, in an application to resting-state fMRI data, the procedure identifies multiple connectivity states, whose occupation times we compare descriptively between the children with combined-type ADHD and the typically developing children used in the fit.
item.dc:creator: Katherine Tsai, Mladen Kolar, Sanmi Koyejo

item.title: A Bayesian approach to the survivor average causal effect in cluster-randomized crossover trials
item.description: arXiv:2505.21447v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In cluster-randomized crossover (CRXO) trials, groups of individuals are randomly assigned to one of two or more sequences of alternating treatments. Since clusters serve as their own control, the CRXO design is typically more statistically efficient than the usual parallel-arm design. CRXO trials are increasingly popular in many areas of health research where the number of available clusters is limited. Further, in trials among severely ill patients, researchers often want to assess the effect of treatments on secondary non-terminal outcomes, but frequently in these studies, there are patients who do not survive to have these measurements fully recorded. In this paper, we provide a causal inference framework and treatment effect estimation method for addressing truncation by death in the setting of CRXO trials. We target the survivor average causal effect (SACE) estimand, a well-defined subgroup treatment effect obtained via principal stratification. We propose causal structural assumptions and standard parametric modeling assumptions that together enable estimating the SACE within a Bayesian paradigm. We evaluate the small-sample performance of our proposed Bayesian approach for estimation of the SACE in CRXO trial settings via simulation studies. We apply our method to a previously conducted two-period cross-sectional CRXO study examining the impact of proton pump inhibitors compared to histamine-2 receptor blockers on length of hospitalization among adults requiring invasive mechanical ventilation.
item.dc:creator: Changjun Li, Dane Isenberg, Michael O. Harhay, Andrew B. Forbes, Paul J. Young, Fan Li, Nandita Mitra

item.title: No Universal Winner in Model Selection: Regression versus Representational Similarity Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2511.00395v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Selecting among competing computational models is central to cognitive psychology and neuroscience, yet the relative model-selection performance of regression and representational similarity analysis (RSA) remains unclear. We compared these approaches using Monte Carlo simulations and empirical data. Univariate simulations compared generating and rival feature models against the same response under direct-linear and geometry-based mappings. Under direct-linear generation, regression outperformed correlation-distance RSA/Spearman but not RSA/Pearson. Under geometry-linear generation, neither approach showed a significant advantage, whereas correlation-distance RSA outperformed regression under a sigmoid readout, although this advantage did not extend to Euclidean-distance RSA. Feature dimensionality, covariance, and PCA preprocessing further influenced model-selection accuracy. In multivoxel simulations, pattern component modeling (PCM) showed superior performance under spatially correlated noise, while crossnobis improved selection relative to squared Euclidean RSA under the same condition. Feature reweighting improved held-out representational correspondence for both generating and rival models without consistently improving model selection. Separate signal-strength comparisons yielded different method rankings. In empirical data from 4,026 words, all methods preferred frequency over affect features, but small-sample preference stability depended on distance measures and preprocessing. Together, these findings demonstrate that model-selection performance depends on stimulus-response mappings, representational geometry, measurement noise, and inferential objectives.
item.dc:creator: Chuanji Gao, Gang Chen, Svetlana V. Shinkareva, Rutvik H. Desai

item.title: Comparative e-backtesting
item.description: arXiv:2511.05840v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Backtesting risk measures is a central task in financial regulation. While traditional backtests evaluate whether a forecasting model is statistically consistent with observed losses, regulatory practice often requires assessing the performance of an internal model relative to standard models. In this paper, we develop a parametric anytime-valid framework for comparative backtests of general risk measures using e-values and e-processes. We construct likelihood-based e-processes for comparative e-backtests with validity and power guarantees. As practical guidelines, we propose the e-three-zone approach based on weak dominance, and introduce the overall and resetting test schemes for different practical purposes. Simulation studies and empirical analyses are conducted to show practical manipulations in financial regulation.
item.dc:creator: Zhanyi Jiao, Qiuqi Wang, Yimiao Zhao

item.title: Who's Afraid of the Wallenius Distribution?
item.description: arXiv:2511.08088v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper is about the use of the Wallenius noncentral hypergeometric distribution for analysing tables generated from a sequential biased sampling scheme without replacement and thus with row margins and sample size fixed. The parameters of the distribution are taken to be weights which are positive and sum to one and are thus defined on a regular simplex. The approach to analysis is presented for likelihood-based and Bayesian inference and is illustrated by example, with datasets taken from the literature or generated from semi-synthetic data. The analysis of the $2 \times 2$ tables using the univariate Wallenius distribution is shown to be straightforward, with the parameter a single weight which translates immediately to the requisite odds and odds ratio. The analysis of tables with more than two categories based on the multivariate Wallenius distribution was however more nuanced than that of the two-category tables. Specifically, some numerical subtleties were required in order to implement the necessary calculations and a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for the Bayesian analysis was introduced.
item.dc:creator: Linda M. Haines

item.title: Environment-Adaptive Covariate Selection: Learning When to Use Spurious Correlations for Out-of-Distribution Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2601.02322v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A common approach to out-of-distribution prediction restricts models to causal or invariant covariates to avoid spurious associations that may change across environments. Despite its theoretical appeal, this strategy can underperform empirical risk minimization when only a subset of the causal parents of the outcome is observed. In such settings, non-causal covariates can serve as proxies for unobserved causal parents and improve prediction when the proxy relationship is stable, but they can hurt when shifts disrupt that relationship. Thus, the optimal covariate set can depend on the specific shift encountered. Because different shifts can leave distinct signatures in the covariate distribution, we propose an environment-adaptive covariate selection algorithm that chooses which covariates to use in each environment based on summaries of its unlabeled covariates. The summaries may be hand-crafted or learned from multi-environment data, and prior causal knowledge can be incorporated as constraints. We give sufficient conditions under which such summaries are informative in linear causal models, and explain when adapting only the covariate set is preferable to letting every coefficient vary with the environment. In simulations and two applications, adapting the covariate set improves prediction over static baselines, including causal and invariant covariate selection.
item.dc:creator: Shuozhi Zuo, Yixin Wang

item.title: Streaming robust covariance estimation and sequential outlier detection
item.description: arXiv:2601.03957v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robust estimation of the covariance matrix and outlier detection remain major statistical hurdles, particularly in large datasets where the rate of data contamination increases. The presence of outliers can severely bias parameter estimates and induce a masking effect, whereby some outliers conceal the presence of other outliers, further complicating their detection. Although many approaches have been proposed for covariance estimation and outlier detection, to our knowledge, none of these methods have been implemented in an online setting. In this paper, we focus on online covariance matrix estimation and outlier detection. Specifically, we propose a new method for simultaneously and online estimating the geometric median and variance, which allows us to calculate the Mahalanobis distance for each incoming data point before deciding whether it should be considered an outlier. To mitigate the masking effect, robust estimation techniques for the mean and variance are required. Our approach uses the geometric median for robust estimation of the location and the median covariance matrix for robust estimation of the dispersion parameters. The new online methods proposed for parameter estimation and outlier detection allow real-time identification of outliers as data are observed sequentially. The performance of our methods is demonstrated on simulated and real datasets.
item.dc:creator: Paul Guillot, Antoine Godichon-Baggioni, St\'ephane Robin, Laure Sansonnet

item.title: Graph Canonical Coherence Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2601.09038v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose graph canonical coherence analysis (gCChA), a novel framework that extends canonical correlation analysis to multivariate graph signals in the graph frequency domain. The proposed method addresses challenges posed by the inherent features of graphs: discreteness, finiteness, and irregularity. It identifies pairs of canonical graph signals that maximize their coherence, enabling the exploration of relationships between two sets of graph signals from a spectral perspective. This framework shows how these relationships change across different structural scales of the graph. We demonstrate the usefulness of this method through a simulation study and an application to economic and energy datasets of G20 countries.
item.dc:creator: Kyusoon Kim, Hee-Seok Oh

item.title: Structure-Adaptive Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Kernel Methods
item.description: arXiv:2602.18958v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimation from observational data in regimes with potentially weak overlap, when the nuisance response functions lie in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), but the contrast function is structurally simpler. We consider three forms of such simplicity: (i) membership in a lower-complexity RKHS with faster eigenvalue decay, (ii) a source condition relative to the nuisance kernel, or (iii) dependence on a known low-dimensional covariate representation. We develop a unified two-stage kernel ridge regression procedure that remains valid under weak overlap and attains minimax rates determined by the complexity of the contrast function. The procedure avoids propensity-score estimation and separate nuisance convergence-rate assumptions. We also show that a simple model-selection step over candidate contrast spaces and regularization levels satisfies an oracle inequality, enabling adaptation to unknown CATE regularity.
item.dc:creator: Seok-Jin Kim

item.title: Causal Network Discovery from Interventional Count Data with Latent Linear DAGs
item.description: arXiv:2603.25838v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The increasing availability of interventional data offers new opportunities for causal discovery, with gene perturbation studies providing a prominent example. Such data are typically count-valued and subject to substantial measurement error arising from technical variability and latent state heterogeneity. Motivated by these challenges, we study identification and estimation in latent linear structural causal models for interventional count data. We propose a latent linear Gaussian directed acyclic graph (DAG) model with Poisson measurement error that explicitly separates the latent causal structure from the observed counts. Under one-sparse mechanism shifts, allowing the structural coefficients and intercept of the targeted gene to change, we establish population-level identifiability of the full latent causal DAG when every node is covered by at least one non-vanishing targeted intervention. Building on these identification results, we develop an estimation procedure based on sparse inverse matrix estimation and provide theoretical guarantees on estimation error and finite-sample causal discovery. Simulation studies and applications to Perturb-seq data demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Yijiao Zhang, Hongzhe Li

item.title: 2D Stability Selection: Design Jittering to Exclude Correlated Irrelevant Variables
item.description: arXiv:2605.02205v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stability Selection finds the variables that are chosen consistently across random subsamples of the data, but it can consistently choose the wrong ones. An irrelevant variable that is strongly correlated with relevant variables can be selected in many subsamples, because resampling the observations does not change the variables themselves. We call such a variable a confounder; the term refers only to this correlation and not to causal confounding. We propose 2D Stability Selection, which also adds random noise to the design matrix, at increasing noise levels, and keeps the variables that are selected throughout. On average, the added noise acts as a ridge penalty, so each fit is a noisy elastic net. This changes the conditions under which the Lasso selects the correct variables: it can restore them when a confounder would otherwise be chosen, and it can also make selection worse. For uncorrelated relevant variables we give an exact criterion for the noise levels at which the population elastic-net irrepresentable condition holds, recovery guarantees for a single fit and for the aggregated procedure, and, for thresholds above $1/2$, a bound on the expected number of false positives (under i.i.d.\ observations; its closed form also needs exchangeable irrelevant variables). In simulations, the method excludes the confounders that Stability Selection includes. In the simulated design, an elastic net used without any noise, with a fixed ridge weight or along a deterministic path, excludes the confounders as well, which suggests that for the Lasso the ridge effect, not the randomness of the noise, is responsible.
item.dc:creator: Mahdi Nouraie, Houying Zhu, Samuel Muller

item.title: A Statistical Framework for Algorithmic Collective Action with Multiple Collectives
item.description: arXiv:2605.06749v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As learning systems increasingly shape everyday decisions, Algorithmic Collective Action (ACA), i.e., users coordinating changes to shared data to steer model behavior, offers a complement to regulator-side policy and corporate model design. Real-world collective actions have traditionally been decentralized and fragmented into multiple collectives, despite sharing overarching objectives, with each collective differing in size, strategy, and actionable goals. However, most of the ACA literature focuses on single collective settings. To address this, we propose the first comprehensive statistical framework for ACA with multiple collectives acting on the same system. In particular, we focus on collective action in classification, studying how multiple collectives can influence a classifier's behavior. We provide quantitative statistical bounds on the success of the collectives, considering the role and the interplay of the collectives' sizes and the alignment of their goals. We make such bounds computable by each collective with only partial knowledge of other collectives' sizes and strategies. Finally, we numerically illustrate our framework on simulations inspired by interventions for climate adaptation in smart cities, demonstrating the usefulness of our bounds.
item.dc:creator: Claudio Battiloro, Pietro Greiner, Dario Rancati, Bret Nestor, Oumaima Amezgar, Francesca Dominici

item.title: An Exact Marginal Likelihood for Inference under Careless Responding
item.description: arXiv:2605.26723v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Careless or insufficient-effort responding threatens the validity of self-report measurement. Mixture models for careless responding specify its form, and screening rules and robust methods depend on a threshold or tuning constant with no direct meaning in terms of careless responses. We propose ExHuber, a Bayesian method for inference on the engaged population under Huber's contamination model, in which an unknown proportion of responses comes from a contaminating distribution of unspecified form instead of the structural model. With a finite support of responses, such as the values of a scale score, a Dirichlet prior and a Beta prior on the contaminating distribution and its proportion yield a closed-form exact marginal likelihood of the structural parameters. Under a prior favoring a contaminating distribution on a few values, we show that the posterior of the structural parameters is consistent when careless responses occupy few values of the support, without knowing which values. Dynamic programming evaluates the marginal likelihood and its gradient at a cost quadratic in the sample size, which enables gradient-based sampling. Simulations from graded response models show accurate inference under straightlining and repeated response patterns, and an application to Big Five scales estimates the engaged mean of each scale.
item.dc:creator: Jaehoan Kim

item.title: Weighted Conformal Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2606.00436v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Clustering is a central tool for discovering latent structure in unlabeled data; yet modern clustering pipelines often end with a hard assignment of each observation to a cluster without rigorous measures of assignment uncertainty. We propose a novel weighted conformal approach for constructing valid confidence sets for cluster labels. The key difficulty is that the labels available for calibration are not observed ground-truth labels, but synthetic labels produced by a data-dependent clustering algorithm. Our method develops a conformal inference algorithm that corrects the resulting mismatch with the latent target labels through weights by formulating conformal clustering as a conditional label-distribution shift problem. We first derive an oracle procedure that attains finite-sample marginal coverage and then develop a computationally tractable and implementable version using estimated conditional label probabilities and novel augmented calibration. We show that the coverage of the estimated-weight procedure depends on the estimator, giving an explicit bound on the loss relative to the nominal level. Empirical studies demonstrate that the proposed weighted approach offers improvements over the recently proposed split conformal clustering procedure in terms of informative confidence set size, especially in nonlinear and high-dimensional clustering applications.
item.dc:creator: Anirban Nath, YoonHaeng Hur, Genevera I. Allen

item.title: Separate versus Pooled Winsorization in Difference-in-Differences: Bias, Efficiency, and Finite-Sample Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2606.15097v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: \textit{\textbf{Problem Definition: }} Extreme outcomes are common in operational data, and empirical difference-in-differences (DiD) studies often winsorize them to limit their influence. Yet winsorization can change both the estimated treatment effect and its sampling uncertainty. We ask when winsorization improves DiD estimation and whether cutoffs should be computed separately within each group-period cell or from observations pooled across cells. \textit{\textbf{Methodology/Results: }} We develop finite-sample and asymptotic analyses in a two-group, two-period DiD setting. For continuous outcomes with finite variance, separate winsorization achieves a uniform sub-Gaussian deviation guarantee under a calibrated winsorization fraction, while neither raw DiD nor pooled winsorization can achieve the same guarantee. We identify conditions under which separate winsorization is asymptotically unbiased, whereas pooled winsorization with a fixed fraction may remain biased. Under these conditions, standard tail classifications alone do not establish an efficiency ranking. Yet a two-sided decreasing-failure-rate (DFR) condition on each cell's error distribution can guarantee strictly smaller asymptotic variance for separate winsorization than for raw DiD at every fixed winsorization fraction. Numerical results support both analyses. \textit{\textbf{Managerial Implications: }} Our results guide practitioners on whether and how to winsorize outcomes in DiD studies, clarifying the advantages and limitations of raw DiD, separate winsorization, and pooled winsorization. The DFR condition arising from our efficiency analysis offers a simple diagnostic for when winsorization can be expected to lower asymptotic variance while keeping the treatment-effect estimate unbiased, giving theoretical grounding to a practice that has so far rested mainly on convention.
item.dc:creator: Chao Cheng (Washington University in St. Louis), Chenshan Hu (University of Colorado Boulder), Yukai Huang (Suffolk University)

item.title: Drift-Aware Spectral Conformal Prediction for Non-Exchangeable Streaming Data: A Controlled Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2606.15953v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Does drift-aware spectral conformal prediction (DASC) narrow the intervals of adaptive conformal inference (ACI) when all methods share one forecaster per data set and one tuning criterion? Not with the projected update. At DASC's step size, projected DASC and ACI widths differ by at most 0.43 per cent on electricity and weather; DASC is wider on finance. With DASC's step size tuned at a larger budget, or with wider step-size sets and scaled bandwidths, paired width intervals against ACI include zero or lie above it. Coverage is near nominal for the adaptive methods, with some under-coverage at the selected settings. The paper contributes a reproducible simulation and resampling design, released with code and saved results: twelve simulated scenarios and three real streams, paired moving-block bootstrap intervals with block-length and seed checks, a perturbation test that every interval uses only past observations (0 failures in 630 checks), and one-at-a-time measurements of how evaluation choices move widths. An earlier preprint reported width reductions of 28 and 42 per cent that came from centring DASC on a different forecast from the baselines. The replacement theory states the status of each result; the earlier long-run theorem was false for the projected update.
item.dc:creator: Jeffery Opoku, David Banahene

item.title: A Fully Specified Bayes Factor Range for Hypothesis Testing and Sensitivity Analysis in Process Tracing
item.description: arXiv:2606.16683v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A Bayes factor can be used in process tracing to reason about the probative value of evidence for a working hypothesis against a rival (Fairfield and Charman 2022). However, relying on the researcher's own sense of probative strength may inflate confidence in $H_1$ (Zaks 2021). We show how to fully specify a generative model of observations to compute Bayes factors in process tracing: First, researchers count the evidence. Second, they classify it as favoring either hypothesis. Third, they formalize a data-generating process that makes the evidence more expected given $H_1$ and another for a rival $H_R$. The ratio of these probabilities yields a fully specified Bayes factor. We compute two Bayes factors under different assumptions, yielding a Bayes factor range that allows researchers to decide whether the balance of evidence favors $H_1$ considering probability thresholds. Our method also facilitates sensitivity analyses of common assumptions, including those about bias and the probative weight of a smoking gun.
item.dc:creator: Matias L\'opez, Jake Bowers, Daniel Gajardo Cooper

item.title: Causal Inference for All: Marginal Estimands for Outcomes Truncated by Death
item.description: arXiv:2607.00222v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In longitudinal studies, outcomes of interest are often truncated by death, meaning that they are only observed or well-defined conditional on intercurrent events such as survival. Existing strategies face a trade-off: causally interpretable estimands, such as survivor average causal effects, target a latent subgroup, whereas while-alive and composite summaries apply to the full population but are difficult to interpret as causal effects on the non-mortality outcome. We address these challenges by introducing methodology for a new set of estimands that (i) concern the entire population, (ii) remain causally interpretable, and (iii) leverage the longitudinal data commonly available in studies with outcomes truncated by death. The set of estimands includes single-world marginal separable effects that generalize conditional separable effects to full-population summaries. We develop identification and estimation results for these estimands and apply the methodology in a reanalysis of a prostate cancer trial, highlighting how different estimands can yield different treatment conclusions.
item.dc:creator: Ruixuan Zhao, Mats Stensrud, Linbo Wang

item.title: Debiased Machine Learning for Partially Linear Accelerated Failure Time Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.07841v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Cox model remains the default for survival analysis, but the proportional hazards assumption is often violated and hazard ratios can be difficult to interpret. Accelerated failure time (AFT) models provide an intuitive time-scale alternative, yet flexible covariate adjustment while preserving valid inference on a target exposure remains challenging. For the partially linear AFT model under right censoring, a rank-based debiased machine learning (DML) framework has not been developed. The rank-based pairwise moment is not Neyman orthogonal, and standard cross-fitting does not directly apply to U-statistics. We develop the first such framework by combining an orthogonalized rank-based U-statistic, a censoring-corrected influence function, and block-pairwise cross-fitting, yielding valid inference for a finite-dimensional exposure effect under flexible machine-learning nuisance estimation. In the primary simulation study, the proposed estimator attains near-nominal coverage under independent and covariate-dependent censoring at rates up to 60%, whereas the nonorthogonal plug-in estimator remains biased. Using All of Us electronic health record data from adults with diabetes and advanced chronic kidney disease, we apply the proposed method to estimate the associations of serum albumin, estimated glomerular filtration rate, and systolic blood pressure with incident cardiovascular outcomes.
item.dc:creator: Tomoki Okuno, Sijie Zheng, Brendon Chau, Gang Li, Jin J. Zhou, Hua Zhou

item.title: Exploring complex dependence structures using Bayesian bi-clustering and log-linear graphical modelling
item.description: arXiv:2608.22375v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian partitioning is utilised simultaneously on subjects and categorical variables to reveal complex dependence structures. Clusters of variables are referred to as views. Variable selection highlights the variables that drive the clustering of the subjects within each view. We derive theoretical results on the relation between the variables' dependence structure and the inferences derived from bi-clustering. The results relate to marginal independence and conditional independence. Using simulated and real data, we demonstrate the applicability of bi-clustering results in assisting log-linear graphical model determination, leading to the efficient exploration of typically vast model spaces. This work sheds light on the relation between two very different but equally popular Bayesian approaches; mixture modelling, that benefits from a large number of variables, and graphical log-linear modelling, which describes explicitly the variables' dependence structure and allows to evaluate the uncertainty associated with model determination.
item.dc:creator: Michail Papathomas

item.title: Calibration of Time-Varying SEIR Models
item.description: arXiv:2609.23089v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mechanistic epidemic calibration can be sensitive to short-lived reporting anomalies that give a few observations high leverage under least squares (LSQ). We develop direct forward-solver least absolute deviations (LAD) calibration for time-varying susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed models fitted to reporting-interval incidence, with finite-horizon regularity and large-sample results. A phase-aware Monte Carlo study compares LAD and LSQ across three transmission drivers, four epidemic phases, five reporting mechanisms, and four forecast horizons. All 120,000 primary fits converged. LAD was favored in 56.7% of mean-absolute-error comparisons and 57.9% of weighted-interval-score comparisons overall; under isolated spikes, backlog release, or temporary underreporting, these proportions rose to 73.6% and 72.2%, with strong gains near the epidemic peak. Rolling-origin validation on four synthetic RAPIDD Ebola scenarios also identifies settings where LSQ is preferred, demonstrating the framework's ability to distinguish robustness gains from sustained-trend behavior. Multiple uncertainty and identifiability diagnostics, complete code and data, and an interactive application provide a reproducible computational workflow.
item.dc:creator: Yisa Abolade, Yichuan Zhao, Gerardo Chowell

item.title: Quantifying Long-Range Dependence in Object-Valued Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2609.24153v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Object-valued time series, including distributions, covariance matrices, networks, and compositions, lack the linear structure required by conventional autocovariance-based definitions of long memory. We develop an intrinsic framework for defining and estimating long memory in metric spaces of negative type. An isometric embedding yields a centered Hilbert-valued process, and the trace of its lag-covariance operator provides a signed, additive measure of temporal dependence. Crucially, this trace equals the difference between the marginal mean pairwise distance and expected lagged distance, so the framework and its estimators use only distances between the original objects. We define the memory parameter through the nonsummable decay of this trace and show that it coincides with the usual parameter in Hilbert-valued settings. Estimation uses Bartlett aggregates of distance-based lag measures. Estimating the common marginal distance from the same dependent sample induces a common-centering bias in these aggregates. We derive its finite-sample form and propose iterated block-difference corrections, log-ratio and multi-bandwidth log-slope estimators, and a localized self-consistency refinement. We establish consistency, document substantial bias reduction in simulations, and find long-memory evidence in foreign-exchange return distributions and U.S. electricity-generation compositions.
item.dc:creator: Won-Ki Seo, Jiazhen Xu, Han Lin Shang

item.title: A non-parametric estimator for excess recurrent events
item.description: arXiv:2609.26328v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Measuring disease burden is an important part of both public health research and health economics. Some measures of disease burden, such as hospitalisations, are made up of recurrent events. Assessing what events are related to a particular disease is however non-trivial. We extend the notion of relative survival to recurrent events by developing a novel non-parametric estimator. The estimator combines data from some cohort with aggregated population level data to estimate the number of excess recurrent events. Using empirical process theory, we show that the estimator converges weakly to a mean zero Gaussian process under mild regularity conditions, and provide a consistent estimator for the covariance function. We also evaluate the finite sample properties of the estimator through simulations and provide a practical example using data from Swedish patients with rectal cancer.
item.dc:creator: Jonatan Hedberg, Ola H\"ossjer, Caroline Nordenwall, Therese M-L Andersson, Elisavet Syriopoulou

item.title: Multiple change-point detection via bottom-up scanning
item.description: arXiv:2609.31116v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study nonparametric multiple change-point detection for high-dimensional sequences, aiming to identify time points at which the underlying distribution changes. While many existing methods perform well when change-points are well-separated, their performance can deteriorate when structural breaks are densely clustered. To address this challenge, we propose gBottomup, a graph-based bottom-up framework for multiple change-point detection in high-dimensional settings. gBottomup constructs a hierarchical segmentation by proposing merges of adjacent segments and verifying them through an unmerge rule that combines absolute significance with relative local heterogeneity, thereby adaptively refining partitions and estimating the number of change-points. Simulation results demonstrate that gBottomup performs reliably across a range of structural configurations and is particularly effective in frequent change-point settings, where existing top-down procedures may lose sensitivity. We illustrate the proposed method through an analysis of high-dimensional sensor data from an experimental hydraulic system.
item.dc:creator: Jinhyeok Park, Taejoon Yang, Hyeyoung Maeng, Hoseung Song

item.title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14695v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When an outcome is missing not at random, identification is commonly restored by a shadow variable: a covariate that predicts the outcome but is excluded from the response mechanism. The literature treats the first requirement, relevance, as a yes-or-no condition. We make it continuous, parametrizing it by a scalar that scales the shadow variable's entire contribution to the moment conditions, and ask what inference costs as that scalar vanishes. One functional of the inverse weight governs the answer. We characterize it exactly, show that it fixes the effective sample size, and use it to sharpen the rates of the estimator that avoids the weight. The characterization is concrete. Whether the functional saturates or diverges turns not on boundedness of the outcome but on whether the tilting variable has an atom at its essential supremum: a binary outcome saturates, a uniform one does not. It also bounds how far a scanned set reaches, and that reach grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the sample size, so a thousandfold increase buys one unit of tilt while the set to be scanned widens. A reanalyzed credit-scoring study shows the cost: a characteristic an optimizing selector uses cannot satisfy exclusion.
item.dc:creator: Michael B\"ucker

item.title: Comparing randomized trials: a formal approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.14895v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Disagreements between randomized trials that address the same causal question pose challenges for the interpretation and synthesis of evidence. We sketch a causal framework for comparing the results of randomized trials that explicitly accommodates the possibility of trial engagement effects. Using counterfactual outcomes defined under joint interventions on treatment assignment and trial-related actions, we compare trial-native treatment effects with the effects transported from one trial to the population of another in a common target population. We show that standard conditions for transporting treatment effects across trial populations are not sufficient to guarantee agreement between transported and trial-native effects. Agreement additionally requires conditions governing how trial-related actions affect outcome across studies - for example, absence of trial engagement effects, equivalence of such effects across trials, or lack of interaction between trial engagement and treatment assignment. Our framework clarifies potential sources of disagreement across trials and extends existing approaches to study comparison to settings in which trial engagement effects may be present.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Han Chiu, Issa J. Dahabreh

item.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
item.description: arXiv:2610.16947v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Statistical data editing in official statistics must restore consistency while limiting changes to observed data. Exact minimum-change correction can be computationally demanding. This paper develops a general framework for structured data whose dependencies admit a normalized acyclic routing representation. It connects routing metadata and explicitly specified semantic edits to logical admissibility, violation diagnosis, and correction. Under stated record semantics, the generated Horn theory characterizes admissibility without materializing its deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the origin of each requirement and identify the variables that can affect a violation. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible records within the specified domain. This characterization is independent of the correction procedure and provides both an objective for correction and a certificate: a verified zero-energy output is admissible and globally minimizes violation energy within its permitted candidate domain. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates based on attained lower bounds. A household survey application illustrates the construction, the verification of admissible corrections, and minimum-cost certification for a subset of outputs. The framework supports traceable validation and correction in official statistics, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.
item.dc:creator: Pierpaolo Massoli

item.title: Renewable model averaging for generalized linear models
item.description: arXiv:2610.33665v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prediction is one of the most important research topics in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, in the domain of streaming data analysis, real-time prediction has become a rapidly growing research field in recent years, owing to the abundance of streaming data. In many fields of scientific research, such as biomedical research, weather forecasting, and traffic management, improving real-time prediction of streaming data is crucial in general. However, the complicated features of streaming data, such as large-scale and high-velocity, impose both theoretical and computational challenges to the development and evaluation of real-time prediction in this field, especially when the investigator has multiple models at hand. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel Renewable Model Averaging method through Quadratic approximation (ReMAQ) for generalized linear model (GLM) for streaming data. By approximating the model averaging procedure for GLMs (which is typically a convex optimization problem) with a quadratic optimization formulation, ReMAQ allows us to update the model averaging prediction sequentially when a new batch of data arrives, without accessing the entire historical data. Moreover, ReMAQ is also computationally efficient as one only needs to consider a quadratic programming problem in each steps of updating. Under certain regular conditions, we also show that the proposed ReMAQ weight is asymptotically equivalent to that by the oracle model averaging based on the inaccessible full data, the asymptotic optimality of ReMAQ is then established accordingly. The proposed method is also assessed by simulation studies. We apply our proposed ReMAQ in the study of the Airline On-Time Performance Dataset and the results demonstrate the superiority our method in practical situations.
item.dc:creator: Yalu Ping, Chen Xuerong, Yu Dalei

item.title: A Sphericity Filter for Space-Filling Designs in Noisy Experiments, with Application to Constrained Mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2610.36012v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Space-filling designs support flexible modeling in noisy multi-response experiments, where some responses may follow simple relationships with factors even when others are complex. An individual design can nevertheless give poor joint precision for low-order effects. We use a low-order working model to guard against such designs while retaining flexibility in the final response analysis. The filter selects one complete candidate from a pool by minimizing geometric loss divided by sphericity, without altering its points. Sphericity measures the balance of the confidence ellipsoid's principal-axis variances independently of its volume. It is the A-criterion's shape factor in the stated coefficient coordinates (raw filtering) and the I-criterion's shape factor in coordinates orthonormal over the prediction region (target filtering). In cube studies with quadratic least-squares and Gaussian-process fits, target filtering reduced aggregate root-mean-square prediction error by 1.4 to 3.3% relative to the geometrically best candidate in the same pool, at a median geometric-loss increase of 0.61%. Its primary benefit is tail protection: in one near-saturated setting, the worst-decile mean working-model prediction standard error fell by about a quarter, at a median geometric-loss increase of 3.2%. In constrained mixtures, raw filtering and A-optimality in physical-proportion Scheffe coordinates can emphasize extrapolated pure-component responses and blending contrasts over regional prediction. Across seven settings, A-optimal designs had 1.3--3.4 times the mean regional working-model prediction variance of I-optimal designs; target filtering improved regional working-model precision in most settings.
item.dc:creator: Andrew T. Karl

item.title: Graph Fourier Neural Kernels: Learning Full PDE Trajectories Across Geometries and Anisotropic Parameter Fields
item.description: arXiv:2410.04655v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-fidelity simulations of time-dependent nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) are expensive to repeat across families of domains and parameter fields, a cost that recurs in design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and computational medicine. Most neural-operator surrogates require each domain to be mapped onto a common grid or reference shape, and few predict the full time course. We introduce Graph Fourier Neural Kernels (G-FuNK), a neural operator for second-order semilinear PDEs with a diffusive principal part that transfers across geometries and anisotropic diffusion tensors without coordinate maps or diffeomorphisms. A weighted graph and its Laplacian supply a spectral basis that encodes geometry and anisotropy. Shared layers act in this basis, at a cost linear in mesh size after one partial eigendecomposition per geometry, and a neural ODE integrator propagates the learned generator to full spatiotemporal trajectories on unseen domains. Across anisotropic heat flow, stiff reaction-diffusion, FitzHugh-Nagumo, and patient-specific left-atrial electrophysiology on CT-derived surfaces, G-FuNK reproduces held-out trajectories with relative $L^2$ error between 0.046 and 0.160. Its accuracy is comparable to that of a geometry-aware Fourier neural operator on regular domains, and its predictions are unchanged when a rectangular domain is rotated. On left atria, whose venous and valvular openings prevent mapping onto a reference shape, it predicts an 85-ms trajectory in under half a second, against about 5 minutes for finite elements, with a mean activation-time error of 1.73 ms. Accuracy depends on graph construction and is highest when the learned generator is integrated at its training time step.
item.dc:creator: Shane E. Loeffler, Zan Ahmad, Shiyi Chen, Syed Yusuf Ali, Carolyna Yamamoto, Kensuke Sakata, Dan M. Popescu, Alana Yee, Yash Lal, Natalia Trayanova, Mauro Maggioni

item.title: Covariate-Adjusted Deep Causal Learning for Heterogeneous Panel Data Models
item.description: arXiv:2505.20536v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper studies the task of estimating heterogeneous treatment effects in causal panel data models with covariate effects. We propose a novel Covariate-Adjusted Deep Causal Learning (CoDEAL) framework that cohesively deals with the underlying heterogeneity and nonlinearity of both panel units and covariate effects. CoDEAL integrates nonlinear covariate effect components (parameterized by a feed-forward neural network) with nonlinear factor structures (modeled by a multi-output autoencoder) to form a heterogeneous causal panel model. The nonlinear covariate component flexibly captures complex covariate influences on outcomes, and the nonlinear factor decomposition enables CoDEAL to effectively capture both cross-sectional and temporal dependencies inherent in the data panel. This latent structural information is subsequently integrated into a customized matrix completion algorithm, thereby facilitating more accurate counterfactual imputation. Moreover, the use of a multi-output autoencoder explicitly accounts for heterogeneity across units and enhances the model interpretability of the latent factors. We establish theoretical guarantees on the convergence of the estimated counterfactuals and demonstrate the compelling performance of the proposed method using extensive simulation studies and real-world data applications.
item.dc:creator: Guanhao Zhou, Yuefeng Han, Xiufan Yu

item.title: funOCLUST: Clustering Functional Data with Outliers
item.description: arXiv:2508.00110v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Functional data present unique challenges for clustering due to their infinite-dimensional nature and potential sensitivity to outliers. An extension of the OCLUST algorithm to the functional setting is proposed to address these issues. The approach leverages the OCLUST framework, creating a robust method to cluster curves and trim outliers. The methodology is evaluated on both simulated and real-world functional datasets, demonstrating strong performance in clustering and outlier identification.
item.dc:creator: Katharine M. Clark, Paul D. McNicholas

item.title: Guaranteed Noisy CP Tensor Recovery via Riemannian Optimization on the Segre Manifold
item.description: arXiv:2510.00569v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recovering a low-CP-rank tensor from noisy linear measurements is a central challenge in high-dimensional data analysis, with applications spanning tensor PCA, scalar-on-tensor regression, tensor-on-tensor regression, and beyond. We exploit the intrinsic geometry of rank-one tensors by casting the recovery task as an optimization problem over the Segre manifold, the smooth Riemannian manifold of rank-one tensors. This geometric viewpoint yields two powerful algorithms: Riemannian Gradient Descent (RGD) and Riemannian Gauss-Newton (RGN), each of which preserves feasibility at every iteration. Under mild noise assumptions, we prove that RGD converges at a local linear rate, while RGN exhibits an initial local quadratic phase followed by linear refinement to the statistical error. Extensive synthetic experiments validate these convergence guarantees and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.
item.dc:creator: Ke Xu, Yuefeng Han

item.title: Identification-aware Markov chain Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2511.12847v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In Bayesian analysis, a proper posterior can exist even when identification fails, but its existence does not ensure reliable posterior computation. More broadly, posterior simulation can be slow when local samplers must move between separated regions or along ridges and weakly curved directions. We develop identification-aware Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers that combine local updates with moves across observationally equivalent parameter values, thereby giving identification analysis a constructive role in modern Bayesian analysis. Under uniform mixing and communication conditions, we establish spectral-gap comparisons in which local-sampler upper bounds vanish as modes separate or likelihood-flat fibers expand, while lower bounds for identification-aware samplers remain bounded away from zero. Simulations illustrate these mechanisms. Structural vector moving-average (SVMA) applications at two scales demonstrate substantial sampling improvements under weak priors, with limited additional gains under strong priors.
item.dc:creator: Toru Kitagawa, Yizhou Kuang

item.title: Statistical Inference for Rates of Change in Spatial Processes over Riemannian Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2601.02305v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Statistical inference for spatial processes from partially realized or scattered data has seen voluminous developments in diverse areas ranging from environmental sciences to business and economics. Inference on the associated rates of change has seen some recent developments. The literature has been restricted to Euclidean domains, where inference is sought on directional derivatives, rates along a chosen direction of interest, at arbitrary locations. Inference for higher order rates, particularly directional curvature has also proved useful in these settings. Modern spatial data often arise from non-Euclidean domains. This manuscript particularly considers spatial processes defined over compact Riemannian manifolds. We develop a comprehensive inferential framework for spatial rates of change for such processes over vector fields. In doing so, we formalize smoothness of process realizations and construct differential processes -- the derivative and curvature processes. We derive conditions for kernels that ensure the existence of these processes and establish validity of the joint multivariate process consisting of the ``parent'' Gaussian process (GP) over the manifold and the associated differential processes. Predictive inference on these rates is devised conditioned on the realized process over the manifold. Manifolds arise as polyhedral meshes in practice. The success of our simulation experiments for assessing derivatives for processes observed over such meshes validate our theoretical findings. By enhancing our understanding of GPs on manifolds, this manuscript unlocks a variety of potential applications in machine learning and statistics where GPs have seen wide usage. We propose a fully model-based approach to inference on the differential processes arising from a spatial process from partially observed or realized data across scattered location on a manifold.
item.dc:creator: Didong Li, Aritra Halder, Sudipto Banerjee

item.title: Partition Tree: Conditional Density Estimation over General Outcome Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2602.04042v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose Partition Tree, a tree-based framework for conditional density estimation over general outcome spaces that supports both continuous and categorical variables within a unified formulation. Our approach models conditional distributions as piecewise-constant densities on data-adaptive partitions and learns trees by greedily minimizing a surrogate for conditional log-loss. This yields a scalable alternative to existing probabilistic trees that does not make parametric assumptions about the target distribution. We further introduce Partition Forest, an ensemble extension obtained by averaging conditional densities. Empirically, we demonstrate improved probabilistic prediction over CART-style trees and competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art probabilistic tree methods and Random Forests.
item.dc:creator: Felipe Angelim, Alessandro Leite

item.title: Maximin Robust Bayesian Experimental Design
item.description: arXiv:2603.14094v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We address the brittleness of Bayesian experimental design under model misspecification by formulating the problem as a max--min game between the experimenter and an adversarial nature subject to information-theoretic constraints. We demonstrate that this approach yields a robust objective governed by Sibson's $\alpha$-mutual information~(MI), which identifies the $\alpha$-tilted posterior as the robust belief update and establishes the R\'enyi divergence as the appropriate measure of conditional information gain. To mitigate the bias and variance of nested Monte Carlo estimators needed to estimate Sibson's $\alpha$-MI, we adopt a PAC-Bayes framework to search over stochastic design policies, yielding rigorous high-probability lower bounds on the robust expected information gain that explicitly control finite-sample error.
item.dc:creator: Hany Abdulsamad, Sahel Iqbal, Christian A. Naesseth, Takuo Matsubara, Adrien Corenflos

item.title: Amortized Vine Copulas for High-Dimensional Density and Information Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2604.20568v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modeling high-dimensional dependencies while keeping likelihoods tractable re- mains challenging. Classical vine copulas provide an explicit dependence structure but require repeated, costly bivariate fitting. We propose Vine Denoising Copula (VDC)1, an amortized estimator for simplified vines on continuous data. VDC trains a single bivariate denoising network on simulated copulas and reuses it across all vine edges. For each edge, the network maps an empirical histogram to a density grid, and iterative proportional fitting approximately enforces uniform grid marginals. The predicted densities and cached conditional transforms support stan- dard vine recursion, likelihood evaluation, sampling, and information estimation. This retains the classical vine factorization while replacing repeated per-edge fitting with reusable neural inference. Across synthetic and real-data benchmarks, VDC combines accurate bivariate density estimation, competitive information estimates, and faster high-dimensional vine fitting after pretraining. Performance varies across datasets; finite grid resolution and conditional prediction remain limitations. The explicit fitted structure supports edge- and tree-level information decomposition, making repeated dependence analysis more practical.
item.dc:creator: Houman Safaai

item.title: Conformalized Super Learner
item.description: arXiv:2604.22391v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Super Learner (SL) is a widely used ensemble method that combines point predictions from a library of learners based on their predictive performance. Interval predictions are of considerable practical interest because they allow uncertainty in predictions produced by an individual learner or an ensemble to be quantified. Several methods have been proposed for constructing interval predictions based on the SL, however, these approaches are typically justified using asymptotic arguments or rely on computationally intensive procedures such as the bootstrap. Conformal prediction (CP) is a machine learning framework for constructing prediction intervals with finite-sample and asymptotic coverage guarantees under mild conditions. We propose coupling CP with the SL through a natural construction that mirrors the original SL framework, using individual learner weights and combining learner-specific conformal prediction sets via a weighted majority vote. We characterize the properties of the resulting SL-based prediction intervals for continuous outcomes. We cover settings under exchangeability, and data-generating mechanisms exhibiting heteroscedasticity, sparsity, and other forms of distributional heterogeneity. A comprehensive simulation study shows that the conformalized SL achieves valid finite-sample coverage with competitive performance relative to the true data-generating mechanism. We present an application of this methodology to predict creatinine levels using socio-demographic, biometric, and laboratory measurements. This example demonstrates the benefits of an ensemble with carefully selected learners designed to capture key aspects of complex regression functions, including non-linear effects, interactions, sparsity, heteroscedasticity, and robustness to outliers.
item.dc:creator: Zhanli Wu, Fabrizio Leisen, Miguel-Angel Luque-Fernandez, F. Javier Rubio

item.title: Express Language Modeling
